I have lived for a good many years in a town where the lighting system and the waterworks have been taken over by the municipality; and while we have disagreed as to details in many things, I must say that the management has been just as good, it not a little better, than under private companies, and the people have always felt that, whatever money was expended, it was their money and it was their business; and the public have taken a greater interest in the management of these public utilities than they did when they belonged to private companies. Then we have the work of the Hydro-Electric Commission in Ontario, which has been Government of a great public utility. That commission has served, and is serving, a useful purpose. I say, without any hesitation, that I believe the establishment of that commission and its working out has brought about the betterment of conditions 20 years sooner than this betterment would have been brought about had there been no Government control of this great public undertaking. I have no fear of the nationalization of railways. It will have to be a complete proposition embracing them all, if it be done at all. Perhaps, as I have said, taking over one or two at a time might be the initial step towards further enlargement of the national system until it would embrace all existing systems. But I do want to make my position clear that I am precluded as a member of this House from moving a resolution that I desire to move, 
imposing conditions on both these companies when we are granting aid to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It appeared to the Government that it was not necessary to proceed by resolution with this Bill as was done in 1914 when the mortgage of $45,000,000 was given to the Canadian Northern Railway Company. This legislation-because it is legislation notwithstanding that the loans are embodied in the Estimates-provides for the. issue of no securities. It is a simple money loan, a lo,an of $15,000,000 upon conditions set out in the Estimate. No. securities are to be issued, no complicated legislation is necessary; and it seems to me, arguing the matter from the standpoint of the right of the Government to introduce this legislation in this way, it is simply a question as to whether or not those proposals are properly in the Estimates. I do not think that the Chairman or the Speaker of the House would rule that these items in the Estimates are out of order. If they are in order, then the Government is clearly within its rights in bringing down, these loans in the Estimates, as has been done.
Does my hon. friend remember the Scripture quoted by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) the other evening, "All things are right; but all things are not expedient"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the Minister of Trade and Commerce quoted Scripture, I would pay more attention to him than to my hon. friend in doing so. There is no reason why the suggestion of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), and the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), should not be discussed, notwithstanding that no power of amendment exists in Committee of Supply. The hon. member for Assiniboia raised the matter the other night. He asked:
Whether, if this vote of $15,000,000 for the Canadian Northern carries, he intends to ask them to hand over to the Government, in addition to the 40 per cent of the common stock of the company that the Government now owns, additional stock to the amount of say $15,000,000 or $20,000,000.
That is the idea the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has in his mind.
Either that or the proposition of the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett); I am not particular.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
At all events, the idea is to obtain control of the stock of the company. The hon. member for Assiniboia went on to say:
I suggest this not because I consider that this stock would be of any particular value, but in order that the Government might be ready to handle the situation and be in a position to avoid being taken by the throat in connection with the matter in the future.
I desire to draw attention in this connection to the legislation of 1914. Under that legislation, in event of default on the part of the Canadian Northern' railway in the payment of interest upon its securities, or in the event of a receivership, which would be in event of default, then this Government has the power, as that legislation is existing to-day, to appoint a board of directors of the Canadian Northern Railway Company and of its subsidiary and constituent -companies to enforce its security; to
-declare the equity of redemption of the Canadian Northern and of all other persons whomsoever in the mortgaged premises to be foreclosed, and thereupon the equity of redemption of thd Canadian Northern (and of such other persons) in the mortgaged premises and every part thereof shall be and become absolutely barred and foreclosed, and the same shall thereupon be vested in His Majesty in right of the Dominion of Canada, any statutory enactment or any rule of law or equity to the contrary notwithstanding.
The effect of that enactment, which is in existence to-day, is that, in the event o-f default on the part of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, so far from the Canadian Northern Railway Company being able to take this Government by the throat, the Government cam demand that the directors of the Canadian Northern Railway system resign their offices, and the Dominion Government may appoint directors in their places, may take complete control of the Canadian Northern Railway system; and may foreclose the equity of redemption of the Canadian Northern rail-' way and deal with that equity of redemption as Parliament may see fit, in the interests of the people of Canada. That was the legislation brought down in 1914 in connection with the guarantee which we then gave upon the $45,000,000 securities of the Canadian Northern. In so far as my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) has declared that the Canadian Northern railway can take this Government by the throat and control the situation, I desire to draw his attention, and the attention of the hon. member for South Renfrew, to the legislation to which-I have referred.
250	.

Would that not mean that the Government would have to take foreclosure proceedings? That would take at least a year, if not more. It would mean, if the Canadian Northern people fought the ease, a long, tedious legal struggle, whereas the whole trouble could be avoided and the Government could be put in a position to act quickly and thoroughly if they controlled this stock. When my hon. friend the Minister of Finance gave the grant of $45,000,000 and the guarantee in 1914, he took over $40,000,000 worth of stock. Now that the company comes for another $15,000,000 more, why not take over another portion of the stock?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend still misunderstands the legislation of 1914. So far from any delay being open to the railway company, under that legislation the Dominion Government can at once appoint boards, take possession, and administer the system by these boards. It has as full power ^s if it had all the stock of the Canadian Northern railway and its subsidiary and constituent companies.
I come to the amendment which my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pu-gsley) had in view. No point of order was taken by myself, or, so far as I know, by any other member of the Government. The point of order was raised by -the Speaker himself'. Personally, I had no objection to the amendment; in fact, I came to the House to-day prepared to discuss it, because it had not occurred to me that it was out of order. The Chairman is, however, clearly right, and no amendment is possible under the rules of the House, but that does not preclude us from discussing the merits of the amendment which my hon. friend from St. John had in view. In that amendment he suggested:
Before making such loan the Governor in Council shall require the company to give His Majesty the King an option to acquire at any time within five years from the date thereof the railways and other property of the company and of all other railways and property included in the Canadian Northern system at such price as to the Governor in Council may seem reasonable under existing circumstances.
That is to say, my hon. friend from St. John had this in view, that, before extending this aid, by way of loan, the Governor in Council should now fix a price at which it would be open to the Government to take over the Canadian Northern system, and that in reaching a conclusion as to that price they should refer to the existing circumstances. I would point out to my hon.



friend that he is dealing there with the equity of redemption of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. Of course, so far as the terms of his amendment go, it would be possible for the Government to, fix a price, $380,000,000 or $400,000,000, or more, but included in that price, of course, would be the debt which the Government would have to assume in taking over the system. My hon. friend will agree that as there are liabilities amounting to some $380,000,000 upon the Canadian Northern system, what the Government would have to do would be to practically fix the value of the equity of redemption of the Canadian Northern railway system in its undertaking; in other words, to fix a fair price upon the value of the stock. That is what the amendment of my hon. friend comes to, and the question arises as to whether it would be wise for the Government, dealing with this matter as it is now dealing with it, to fix a price at which it would be within the power of the Government within the next five years to take over the Canadian Northern Railway system. It has to be pointed out that at present the Government holds 40 per cent of the stock of the Canadian Northern, that is to say, $40,000,000 out of a total issued capital stock of $100,000,000. My hon. friend from Assiniboia says that there is no value in the stock, but he and my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) are evidently at variance as to that, because it is perfectly clear that my hon. friend from St. John, by reason of the suggestion that the Government should fix an option, has in mind that there is value in the stock of the Canadian Northern to-day. He is at variance with the hon. member for Assiniboia, who says that the stock has absolutely no value, and whose suggestion was that the Government might be better able to control, through a majority interest in the stock, the administration of the Canadian Northern Railway system.
Purely voting.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, purely voting. I have pointed out that the holding of a majority interest in the stock is not necessary to enable us to control the Canadian Northern Railway system in the event of default, and if we took over to-day the administration of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, no default having taken place, we should not only have to provide this $15,000,000, which we are providing by way of a loan so as to meet the temporary obligations of the Canadian Northern system, but we would also have to take upon

ourselves the burden of financing the Canadian Northern system during the present war and hereafter.
Hon, gentlemen will have observed from the statements laid before the House the position of the Canadian Northern-$92,000,000 of maturities this year and next year, and obligations current. The sum of $15,000,000 is the minimum amount, upon receiving which by way of loan the Canadian Northern will be able to finance the obligations which it has still to meet during the present and the coming year. The Government is not at this moment proposing to control the operation of the Canadian Northern, because if it did propose to control it, it would have to undertake the burden of financing the Canadian Northern system. The proposals of the Government are to assist the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Railway Company by way of loans of minimum amount, upon receiving which, the two railway companies will be able to continue their operation during the present war. It is a temporary measure designed to enable these two companies to go on as solvent concerns, until we can make the investigation to which I alluded in my speech upon the occasion of the House going into committee on this subject, until we can make an investigation into the whole of the Canadian railway situation, so that we can substitute for the temporary policies which have been adopted during recent years a permanent policy which will, we hope, solve the whole railway situation.
To come back to the question of taking an option, under the legislation of 1914, in the event of default, the Government may foreclose, and it will then be for Parliament to say whether they will pay anything for equity of redemption or not. It will be open to Parliament to say:	We
shall pay something or we shall pay nothing. There is another feature. Not only do we control the situation through the legislation of 1914, but, as pointed out by the hon. member for Calgary, we absolutely control it by reason of the fact that this $15,000,000 loan is a demand loan, and being a demand loan, we hold a stronger position than if we held a majority of the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company because the rights of a creditor are higher than the rights of a shareholder. The company not being able to meet his demand, the creditor absolutely controls the situation. So that from a strictly legal standpoint it is not necessary that we should have a majority of the stock of the

Canadian Northern railway in order to control the administration of that road in case of default.
Is it intended to exercise the right of calling in this $15,000,000 in case of default?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have told my hon. friend that the Government is investigating the whole Canadian railway situation. We are doing what I believe is the sensible thing under present -conditions. The Canadian railway situation is exceedingly complicated and one of the most important that has ever confronted any Government in Canada. We are taking the opinion of experts, and when we have their advice we shall be in a position to act. In the meantime, by reason of this being a demand loan, our position is such that we can control the situation. There is another point. Hon. gentlemen have suggested that we should obtain control of the Canadian Northern railway stock. Now, it must be borne in mind that the possession of that stock is very valuable to them in financing the Canadian Northern railway system. As a matter of fact, I understand that to-day their stock is pledged in order to assist in the financing of the company. The company, of course, has to continue to finance itself, and it seems to me that as we are affording the minimum degree of assistance with which the company can get on, we should not take any step that would prevent the Canadian Northern railway from doing its share of the financing. As the hon. member for Assiniboia thinks the stock has no commercial value-and I am not pronouncing upon that at all-the only point my hon. friend can have in mind is the control of the Canadian Northern system, and I have already pointed out that we have that control by the legislation of 1914 and by reason o!r the fact that this is a demand loan. There is another aspect that I commend to, the attention of the hon. member for St. John. Would it be wise for the Government at this time to place a value upon Canadian Northern stock? If we did that we should have to say that the stock was either worth nothing, at all or worth a small amount, or perhaps a large amount. Now if the stock was not worth anything, as my hon. friend from Asiniboia thinks, whaJt would be the use of taking an option on it?

No use except that it
would give you control.
250i

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have dealt
with control. Again, if the Government put a small value upon the stock, that would unquestionably embarrass the Canadian Northern in the financing which they must do to carry on this road, for I have already stated that the stock is of value to them in carrying on their financing. So if the Government, taking the advice of the hon. member for St. John, placed a small value on the stock and took an option on it for five years, we would be fettering the company, or at least the owners of the majority of the stock, in the financing which they and the company have to do if the company is to continue as a going concern. If the Government took the other alternative and put a large value on the stock, what would be the position if by reason of default the Government found it necessary to take over the Canadian Northern railway system? Under the legislation of 1914 it would then be for Parliament to determine what should be done with the road and how much should be paid to the stockholders, whether anything or nothing. Why should the Government take a step which might embarrass Parliament in dealing with the equity of redemption should the road ever default? Unquestionably the placing of a value on the stock would fetter the Government in deciding what should be done with the equity of redemption, if it had to deal, with it under the legislation of 1914.
So far as control is concerned, I have shown that we are able to exercise all the control we need under the legislation of 1914 and by reason of the fact that this is a demand loan. I have shown further that the taking of this stock by the Government would seriously embarrass the Canadian Northern railway and its shareholders in the very necessary work of carrying on the financing of this road. The Canadian Northern railway financial arrangements are not going to be completed by obtaining this $15,000,000 from the Government. There are the maturing obligations of this and next year and current liabilities to be met to the amount of $92,000,000.
How will possession of the common stock which stands behind all this security assist the company in their financing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows that in the eyes of financial men the majority of the stock of a company like the Canadian Northern railway might be

regarded as of considerable value as additional collateral. It might make just the difference between the company obtaining a loan and not obtaining a loan. As a matter of fact, I understand that the stock is now pledged for that very purpose.	,

Has it a market value
to-day?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know whether it has or not. But my hon. friend evidently has it in mind that it has, or he would not suggest that the Government fix a price at which it could take over the road at any time during the next five years.
What I am afraid of is that after the Government has pulled the road through, the stock will have a vast prospective value.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Where would have been the difficulty, after this Government came into power, in arranging to give the Canadian Northern running rights through the mountains over the Grand Trunk Pacific, instead of giving them the subsidy and joining the British Columbia Government, which guaranteed bonds for over $40,000,000 to enable them to build an independent line down through the Rockies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The line was under construction. Not only that, as I pointed out the other evening-

They started construe

tion on the British Columbia grant.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. ' ' \
But is it not true they had no assistance from Canada to go through the Rocky mountains?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The line was under construction when we gave the assistance. In the legislation of the late Government, under which a grant of $35,000,000 [DOT]was given on the Canadian Northern Ontario line between Montreal and Port Arthur, it was recited that it was in the interest of Canada that there should be a third transcontinental line from Montreal to the waters of the Pacific. It was that $35,000,000 grant on the Canadian Northern Ontario line between Montreal and Port Arthur that determined the character of the Canadian Northern as a transcontinental system. There is not a doubt about that, and at the time that grant was given the late Government had in contemplation, and stated in the recital of the resolution, that it was in the public interest that the line should be carried through to British Columbia to reach the waters of the Pacific.
There is one thing about this debate that has pleased me, and that is that there has been very little recrimination. The past is a closed book. I address myself to this railway situation with no favourites. It is one of the most important situations that has ever confronted any Government in this country; it has been for the last four years. The difficulty in this country as we all know is the immense geographical area and the sparseness of our population. In the early days confederation was possible only because the Intercolonial, built at great expense, linked up the then East with the then West. The next great step taken was the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway which made a larger confederation possible, and linked up the West and British Columbia with the East. Then we had the building of the Canadian Northern railway in the Prairie Provinces. And there is one aspect of this that is apt to be overlooked, .and that is the enormous importance to Canada of the railway situation which we have built up. Almost every day in this House we hear, of the necessity of more transportation, of more cars-, of new districts in the West that should be reached

by branch lines. What would be the condition in the West to-day if those lines had not been built.
Deplorable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Last year 40 per cent of the wheat was carried out by the Canadian Northern Railway system. This question is not a matter of individuals ; it is not a matter of the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian Northern or the Grand Trunk Pacific as a corporation. The point is, the importance of the railway system to Canada and its development; and that is the way in which this question ought to be approached. What we have before us to-day is not a theory but a condition. We have these three railway systems completed-except that railway systems.are never completed, because they must always extend, must always increase their mileage as conditions permit. No question in this country since Confederation has been so vital to it as that of the railways. My own opinion is that we have overbuilt for the time being. But it must be borne in mind that public opinion has been in favour of building railways, to connect the East and the West, to develop the West, and to afford access to the remoter parts of the country in order that immigration might flow in and settlement result. The whole country has benefited'by .the extension of the railway systems to tthe West. Therefore,, though, as I say, we Lave overbuilt, it must not be forgotten that the most vital question in this country today is the transportation question. That being the case, I personally do not believe in getting into a pessimistic frame of'mind with regard to Canada. If, when this war broke out, anyone had-told me as Minister of Finance that we should have been in the condition in which we are to-day the war having lasted almost two years, I should not have believed it. Consider the position of Canada oo-d'ay. Notwithstanding this war, Canada enjoys a very high degree of prosperity. Our exports are greatly in excess of our imports, and our trade is the largest this country has ever had. Our bank deposits are two or three hundred millions greater than they were at the outbreak of the war. I do not allow myself to take too long views of things, because I do not believe that the human mind is capable of forecasting what will take place after this war is over. I have great confidence in the people of this country and in this country's resources, and so I do not

allow myself to think things are going to the bad after this war is over.

They don't give any
reasons.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, they do not. I rely with the greatest confidence upon Canada's .ability to carry out her share in this war and to come through the war with a high degree of prosperity.
In connection with the hon. minister's financial operations, which have been very successful, does he not find himself hampered sometimes by the pessimistic remarks made by his colleagues?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
Has the hon. minister
any view as to a broad immigration policy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have. At the present time the sources of immigration are largely stopped by reason of the war. But not only should the Government use every effort to promote immigration, it should encourage any auxiliary means there may be of bringing in immigration; it should seek to have its own efforts to
bring immigration intp this country supplemented by the efforts of others. In addition to that, once the immigration is here, the Government should assist, by some plan that I think could be devised, in getting the people settled on the land.

To my mind this is the most important question we have had to deal with. I am glad the minister has touched upon the subject of immigration. The minister has stated that the sources of immigration are stopped during the war. Is that true in regard to the vast multitude of people to the south of us, in the United States, from which in recent years we have obtained hundreds of thousands of our very best settlers? Why should we not, by a vigorous policy, continue to get people from the United States even in larger numbers than in the past?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend is right so far as the United States is concerned. When I spoke of the sources of immigration being stopped, I had reference rather to European sources. -Jit the same time, we must not disguise the fact that the war has an influence upon immigration even from the south. It is not rational that it should be so, but it is a fact, nevertheless.
I have shown the railway situation which confronted this Government when it came into power. I have indicated my views as to the importance of the problem, and to the unwisdom of allowing these railway systems which have continued up to the present time to collapse. I have indicated my faith that the country with its resources and with its people will overcome any difficulties that may be presented in the future. On the whole, as I have stated, my attitude is one of optimism, not of pessimism, in regard to the future of this country, even of the railways of this country-although I say that in my view we have overbuilt. It must be borne in mind, however, having regard to the geographical areas of this country, that it is, in a sense, necessary to overbuild. That is to say, you do not get your settlement until you get your railway; the railway comes first in order of time. I do not desire, as I have said, to enter upon any controversy, but my view is that if the Canadian Northern Kailway system and the Grand Trunk could have been put together in 1903-4, this overbuilding situation would have been avoided. The Canadian Northern was taking grain out of the West, but the Canadian Northern

must find return traffic, and the reason why the Canadian Northern embarked upon its railway policy in the East was in order to obtain feeders for its western system. If the Canadian Northern had had the Grand Trunk as a feeder in the East, then the Canadian Northern would not have needed1 the Canadian Northern' Ontario; but by reason of the Grand Trunk promoting the Grand Trunk Pacific the Canadian Northern found itself in a position in which it would be shipping grain out of the West but not taking freights back. Consequently, it embarked on the policy of building the Canadian Northern Ontario. As I have said, there is no use in recriminating. There is not much use in criticising. There is not much use in making reflections upon the wisdom or unwisdom of past policies. The fact is that the railway situation, so important to the people of Canada, is here before us and we have to deal with it, and that is what the Government proposes to do.
Some points have been raised as to the disposition of this money. We are making a loan of 815,000,000 to the Canadian Northern Railway Company. Under the legislation of 1914 and of 1911 the Dominion Government gave guarantees of $45,000,000 and $35,000,000 to the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company. The proceeds of those securities went into the Receiver General's account under the legislation in both cases. I have been trustee for hundreds of millions of dollars in my time, and I can say that no more complete check could be devised than was devised by the Railway Department in authorizing the payment out of those moneys. I say here as Minister of Finance that the proceeds of the $45,000,000 guarantee were paid out absolutely for the purposes for which the guarantee was given, and for no other purpose whatsoever.
Was that money handled by Mackenzie and Mann?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A guarantee was given for the purpose of paying indebtedness incurred and expenditures made on construction account and for certain other things mentioned in the legislation. The suggestion has been made in the House that in some mysterious way the money is being diverted, but I say there is not a word of truth in that.
Those suggestions came largely from the other side of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They did not
come from me. I set out in the statement which I laid on the table of the House every single certificate, and at the end I set out a letter from Major Bell, who is an admirable official, one of the best officials in Ottawa-he is an expert accountant-in which he stated that in all cases before these certificates were issued-I am speaking now of the $45,000,000 guarantee-a careful audit was made either by himself or by members of my staff under my supervision. Every voucher was checked; he had representatives even in Winnipeg.

My hon. friend is aware that the great bulk of the Canadian Northern railway was built by Mackenzie and Mann as contractors. The certificate might be perfectly right, but if Mackenzie and Mann charged $50,000 for doing $35,000 wortfi of work, what was the check worth?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was shown in 1914 that nothing of the kind occurred; that they were the agency of the Canadian Northern for making these contracts with sub-contractors. I will say this-after all, the truth' is the truth-I do not believe there is a more economically conducted railway in Canada than the Canadian Northern. I have absolute confidence in the accounts that are presented.
Is there any railroad that has its investments at a cheaper rate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know of any. The proceeds of this $15,000,000 loan are paid over on the order of the Governor in Council. It will be audited just as the. proceeds of the $35,000,000 of guaranteed securities were audited, and as the proceeds of the $45,000,000 of securities were audited. I have had some experience in trust, company work in paying out moneys, and I do not know of any system of any trust company in this country under which the disbursement of moneys are paid out with greater care than the proceeds of Dominion guaranteed securities are paid out at Ottawa. I think that would apply to the late Government as well as to this Government;
I believe that the Finance Department has been absolutely honest in its administration of public funds. This loan will be paid over on the order of the Governor in Couneil after an audit is made to show that it is properly paid out. We are charging 6 per cent, and the loan is a demand loan. I believe that every possible safeguard has been thrown around this transaction from

the standpoint of the Dominion Government. A mortgage is being taken upon the undertaking of the Canadian Northern and its subsidiary and constituent companies which may derive benefit from this loan. Therefore, so far as the transaction itself is concerned, I have no hesitation whatever in supporting and recommending it.
One or two other matters were mentioned, among them the assets of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. The Canadian Northern Railway Company has been built in more recent years than the Canadian Pacific. I do not know what system the Canadian Pacific has in vogue, but if it carries on its business the way other companies carry on their business, I suppose the property values were entered up as of the time that they were acquired. That may also be so in connection with the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and, that being so, the Canadian Northern Railway Company's assets would naturally stand at a much higher figure because they had been acquired in later days. The sums that would be paid for the Canadian Northern Ontario right of way through the province of Ontario would be very large as compared with the cost twenty years previously. If the Canadian Pacific assets were entered up at their present value, I think they would be very much larger than that at which they now appear. I am the first to pay tribute to the Canadian Pacific and the efficiency of its management, but it must not be forgotten that years ago the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was not in as prosperous a condition as it is to-day. Its western lands have become immensely valuable. Its own enterprise, of course, had a great deal'to do with making them valuable, but it must not be forgotten that the enterprise of other concerns also tended to make these lands valuable. So that the Canadian Pacific railway is through its land holdings a participant in the prosperity which was brought about, perhaps, in large measure by itself, but also by these other railway companies, that is tb say, the Canadian Northern, and in less degree the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.

And by the enterprise
of the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And by the enterprise of the people, and by the assistance which the Government of Canada has given to all these enterprises. The hon. member
for South York (Mr. Maclean) the other day spoke, lightly I thought, of taking over all the railway systems of Canada.
Sure; it would only take a minute.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: at the rate of twenty or twenty-fivie million dollars a month, some two hundred and fifty or three hundred million dollars a . year; that we shall probably be confronted with a debt, at the end of this war, of one thousand million dollars. In time of peace it would not be a light undertaking to bring about the nationalization of all the railways of Canada; it would certainly not be a light undertaking to do so in time of war. But this situation must be faced; there must be an encl of this annual coming to the Government of Canada by these two railway companies for relief. The policy which we have adopted has been stated to be no policy. I say it is the true policy in the situation in which we find ourselves. We are not in a position to say what should be the permanent solution of Canada's railway problem. We are in this position, that we do not want these railway companies to collapse. The policy which has been before this committee, and I know it has met with approval in this House, is the true policy at this time, and it is not the less the true policy because it provides temporarily for the situation. It bridges time; it enables these roads to continue- these roads which are so vital, so essential for the welfare of this country-until such time as, upon the best advice that we can get, we shall be able to suggest some permanent solution, which I believe will probably involve the taking over by this Government of one or more of the existing railway systems of Canada, and which, as I stated, may involve later on the nationalization of all the railway systems of Canada.

With the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), I distinctly voice my objection to the manner in which this legislation has been brought up. Even with the explanation of the Minister of Finance as to the whys and wherefores of bringing it before the House in this way, the fact remains that it should have been introduced by resolution. Further than that, I want to wholly endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett). There are many of us who took a somewhat strong position in 1914 in regard to the legislation granting $45,000,000 to the Canadian North, ern railway. It appears to me to be a most vicious practice that practically the largest amount, outside of our civil government, that we grant in this country are to railways, and that invariably-and perhaps one side is not more to blame than the * 
other-the Government waits and waits until the dying d.ays of the session and then such important legislation, with all that attaches to it, is put before this House. I am not going to cavil to any great extent, but we have been here practically for a month waiting for the Government to bring down this railway legislation and it has only just now come down, when everybody is in a mood to finish the session and go home. I am glad to hear the Minister of Finance speak with the optimism he does. We have at the	present	time rather	toomany pessimists	in this	country
Hear,	hear.

-who	are going	along
with their, mouths drawn down and predicting all sorts of evil things for Canada at the end of the war. It is true they all say we are overbuilt in railways. Unquestionably we are; but I would remind this House and the country that for ten years after the Canadian Pacific railway was completed we were also overbuilt. The building of railways in districts where they are most needed, has invariably produced good results. The railways have brought the people, the people have brought prosperity ; and to a large extent the great prosperity of the West is due to the building of the Canadian Pacific railway and the immigration which that railway brought into the West, to such an extent that it has enriched this country by millions and millions of dollars. Then if we had not had the existing railway transportation, even although we were overbuilt, with the abnormal crop of last year in the West, Canada would have been in a far worse position than she is in to-day. So, I am not finding fault to any great extent with the building of the railroad. The only thing that does strike me in regard to the Canadian Northern is that, year after year, we come to this House and, year after year, grants are made to the Canadian Northern Railway and, year after year, the same question is put from either one side of the House or the other:	Is this the last aid that the
Canadian Northern Railway is going to require? And the invariable answer is: Yes, this is all they want; this will see them through. I have been listening to that now for a good many years, and yet, as the sessions roll around, still there come other requests from the Canadian Northern railway: " We are again in deep water; we come to you and ask you to give us aid."
It has become, so far as my observation goes, a question in the country whether or

not the Canadian Northern Railway is being properly managed. We have been told by the Finance Minister that in his opinion- and without any disrespect to him I am sure he will allow me to take his opinion in this matter, for what it is worth, as mine is to be taken-that it is a most economically managed railway, that all the money that comes from this railway goes back into it and that, as a matter of fact, it is properly managed in all respects. That may or may not be true. Speaking for myself, I would like to be convinced by a most thorough independent audit of the Canadian Northern Railway Company's books that all the money that is earned by the Canadian Northern goes back into the Canadian Northern. The hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) fold us this afternoon that $10,000,000 is the estimated profits of the Canadian Northern on its operating account. If that is so, I would like to know, merely as a citizen, if that $10,000,000 goes back into the Canadian Northern. We want to know that, and we can only know that by a better and more independent audit of Canadian Northern affairs than there has been up to the present time. Would it not strike the ordinary man that, having regard to the fact that these requests are coming session after session, and are granted, as this request will be granted, I have no doubt, the Government, not from the point of view of the value of the stock of the Canadian Northern-I care nothing about that for the purposes of my argument-but for the purposes of the management of the Canadian Northern, should take unto itself sufficient stock to give it control, irrespective of the control which it acquired in 1914; that it should appoint upon the Canadian Northern Board men, in whom the people would have confidence, to see that the money which comes from the Canadian Northern goes hack into the Canadian Northern, so that the people would know exactly where the money is going, and, therefore, whether these grants are being made properly or not. That is the point I make. So far as the stock goes, I agree with the minister's argument, so far as it goes, but, to my mind, no argument can be successfully put up against the contention that as the people of this country have advanced, in this Parliament and in other Parliaments, enormous amounts of money, they should know that the moneys which come from the Canadian Northern go back into the Canadian Northern and that the
road is properly managed. This, it would appear to me, is a proper enough request, and it is something that really ought to be done.
So far as I am concerned,-I am expressing only my own opinion-I am in favour of a receivership for the Canadian Northern. A receivership would not dislocate matters in connection with that system to the slightest degree. The borrowing powers would not be curtailed in any way, and the financing of the road would not be hampered in any way. A receiver could go on and do exactly the same thing to-day as if the road were left, as no doubt it will be left, in the hands of the present owners. But there would be this advantage, il submit, that if a receiver were appointed for the Canadian Northern railway, and he was a man in whom the country had confidence, the people would know that, dollar for dollar, the money that was coming in and going out was being applied and expended in the interests of the road, and therefore, in the interests of the people of Canada. The matter is becoming serious, so serious that when we consider the enormous amount of money that has been put into the Canadian Northern railroad, and that the money has to a very large extent been advanced by the people of Canada, it seems high time that the people of the Dominion had a voice in the running and operating of that road. I have not heard any argument advanced by the Minister of Finance against a receivership. I would like to hear, for my own information, whether, in any way the road would be prejudiced by such an appointment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I dealt with the matter in my speech before we went into committee. I pointed out that a receivership would mean by reason of the number of subsidiary companies involved, dismemberment of the system, a break-up.
I would not think that that would be an insuperable difficulty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are thirty or forty of them.	[DOT]
I have yet to be convinced that the hon. minister is right.
Would the hon. gentleman apply the same principle to the Grand Trunk?
It might be veTy reasonable to do the same thing.
In regard to the Grand Trunk and Grand Trunk Pacific ?

The Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific are locked together. If, as the Grand Trunk railway tell us today, the Grand Trunk railway can no longer carry the Grand Trunk Pacific, and if it is a fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific will have to come for aid in subsequent years, in the same way as the Canadian Northern has come, the sooner we take hold of the Grand Trunk Pacific the better. So far as I am concerned, the horn, member for Perth (Mr. Morphy) can take no comfort from the view that because we had to do with the Grand Trunk Pacific we should argue another way. I say that so far as the Canadian Northern is concerned, the control of the stock ought to be taken, that the people ought to have upon that board representatives able to take care of the receipts and expenditures of the road. If this is not done, and I have no doubt it will not be done, I say a receiver should be appointed in whom the people of the Dominion would have confidence, so that they would know exactly whether or not the money which they had invested in that road would be properly expended.
We are told that a commission is to be appointed, "a commission for inquiry and report upon the railway situation," and for that purpose a sum of $150,000 has been placed in the Supplementary Estimates. Since 1911, when this Government came into power, there has been a superfluity of commissions in this country. Some 85 commissions have been appointed for one reason or another, according to a return recently brought down. Some of these commissions have done something; some of them have done very little, but I do think -and I am not speaking in a partisan way-that, before these sums are voted to the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific, it would be fair for the Government to give this House the names of the commissioners who will inquire into the railway systems of the Dominion. That at least would have the effect that, when these votes go through, the country will know that, even although another vast sum had been granted to the Canadian Northern, men in whom they had absolute confidence were being appointed to inquire into the operations and carryings of these two roads, and that, therefore, they might reasonably hope that before another grant is asked, as

no doubt it will be, they would knoiw all the facts connected with these roads.
In conclusion, I just wish to say that I think, and I believe the people of this country think, that before any further large grants are made to the railways, of this country, and especially the Canadian Northern railway, the people should be fully informed of all the facts, and if any railway is to be assisted the Dominion Government should be fully protected so far as the outgoings and incomings of that road are concerned.

I have listened with very great interest to the remarks of my bon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett), and if I appreciated them correctly their logical conclusion was, or might very well be interpreted to be that Canada had reached the limit of its railway development. When he argued that to-day we have far overbuilt in railroads, and are in consequence suffering serious financial difficulties, the logical conclusion of his argument must have been that we should not build in the near future. I maintain that so far as the western country is concerned we are not over-built, and not only are we not overbuilt, but it has been my duty to bring to the attention of the Government from time to time the needs of certain localities for additional railways. I am not alone in that, as other members have been impelled to bring the same aspect of the case to the Government's attention. Admitting, for the sake of argument, that there has been over-building in some directions, there is still a need of further building in other directions. Even if it should be demonstrated to the satisfaction of the country that we have over-built in some districts, that is no reason why we should not have further construction in other places where it is needed. I will not go over the details as to where it is needed, as I have already discussed in the House construction in which my constituency is particularly interested.	[DOT]
First of all, let me say on the general question whether ' we have over-built or not, that in developing a new country we build in advance of requirements ; otherwise there would, be no development through railway construction. It is admitted in the present day and generation that if we have a country to develop it is sound policy to invest the public money and credit in the construction of railways that will secure that develop-

ment; and it is not until after the road has been constructed that development takes place, or can take place. When, therefore, it is said that we have over-built and have not the traffic to make our railways profitable, we are simply stating what must necessarily be the case: the railways must be built before the traffic is created. We build the railway in order to create the traffic, and we must await the natural and ordinary development of the traffic before we can expect a railroad to have the earnings which it will ultimately have. Such a condition does not indicate any fall-down or failure of our policy in railway projects. It is true that war conditions at the moment are preventing, and will prevent, so long as they continue, that expected development upon which we rely for carrying the capital charges and expenses of our roads. But that is an abnormal condition that no foresight could have provided against; that is an abnormal condition that lays serious burdens upon us which we never expected. Those conditions have to be met, and it is now for us to say in what manner we shall deal with them. I do not wish to discuss at the moment how we should deal with this question, but I want to bring to the attention of the House the fact that the railway condition confronting us is not an abnormal or an unnatural one, but the normal and the natural one, except in so far as it has been made abnormal by abnormal war conditions. As my hon. friend from Lamb-ton (Mr. Pardee) has said, we were overbuilt when the Canadian Pacific Railway was completed. It was many years before the traffic that was created by the building of that road was sufficient to make the Canadian Pacific Railway a profitable enterprise. There was less traffic per railway mile in Canada on the day the last rail of the Canadian Pacific railway was laid than there is to-day, counting every mile of railroad we have in the country. Just as the building of the Canadian Pacific railway produced valuable results to the country, which results, however, had to be waited for, so the building of the Transcontinental and the Canadian Northern railways have produced and are producing results, but we must wait a reasonable period for those results to accrue. In fact, it is still in dispute whether the Transcontinental is cpmpleted yet; the Canadian Northern railway is certainly not completed. After the Canadian Pacific railway had been completed across the continent and its branch lines completed to Prince
Albert and Edmonton, it was still ten years, so far as the main line was concerned, and five years so far as the branch lines were concerned, before the road was doing the business that is being done to-day by the Canadian Northern Railway and the Transcontinental.
We are to find the solution of our railway difficulties in increased settlement and development? When we realize that of the crop of last year produced in the prairie West, practically half of that available for export still lies in the elevators and in the granaries of that prairie West- because there were not transportation facilities to move it to the seaboard during the months that have passed, I ask you, Sir, to prove to me that the country is overbuilt with railroads. I do not think the evidence is that the country is overbuilt with railroads. It may be evidence that the railroads are not well managed ;that the business is not well directed; but when such facts are brought before the House as were brought before it the other day by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Cruise) and by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), that men in the prairie West in the month of May, having hauled their grain fifteen or twenty miles to the elevator at the railroad station to sell it, could not sell it because the elevator was full, and that the elevator was full because the railroad had not been able to take away the grain. I say that the evidence has yet. to be produced to show that this country is overbuilt with railroads.
While I do not wish to introduce contentious matters, there must he some question as to responsibility in this ease, and I maintain that the Government of Canada, being responsible for the railway situation, having assumed absolute responsibility for the operation of the Transcontinental, certainly are the people who either should not have allowed that condition to exist or should be able to say to the House why it exists and how they propose to remedy it. Certainly, for the Government to come to the House and ask for loans amounting to $23,000,000 to pay interest and cost on railroads now existing, on the plea that they are not able to earn interest on their bonds owing to lack of traffic, while the prairie West is choked with its own wealth produced last year, is a situation that I maintain demands explanation.
I agree with my hon, friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) when he says that every dollar of this loan should be traced by the Government in order to see that it goes

where it is intended to go, and that there should be no question as to the fact of the money being used to meet the purpose for which it is voted. I supplement that with the criticism that the Government, having had to take this responsibility ever since they have held office having two years ago come before the House and the country with their proposal for a guarantee of $45,000,000 for the Canadian Northern, and having since that time made further advances to both the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific, are not square before the House when they come to us in the face of existing financial conditions of the railroad companies on the one hand and as to the traffic conditions of the country on the other, and give us no word of explanation in the matter and tell us they .are going to appoint a commission to inquire into the whole business. I do not. agree with what my 'hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) and other hon. members on both sides of the House have said as to the appointment of a commission in this matter. This is not a time nor an occasion for the appointment of a commission; it is a time and an occasion for the Government of Canada to come before the people of Canada with a definite policy as to what they propose on their responsibility to do in handling the railroad situation of this country. What can, by any possibility, be the result of any inquiry that may be made? I have already criticised the Government for its attitude towards the Grand Trunk Pacific. I may be misunderstood if I criticise the Government for its attitude towards the Canadian Northern; but I ask: How can any business enterprise, looking for money in the markets of the world; expect to get that money on fair and good terms in the face of the deluge of adverse criticism that both these railway enterprises have received in this House from the Government as well as from the Opposition? How can it be expected that a company shall be successful in financing, that is to say in borrowing money on its credit, if those who are its principal creditors, who have absolute control of it in every particular, discredit it as a well thought out enterprise and discredit its management as well? Both enterprises may deserve everything that is said in regard to them; but that having been said, it is futile to say that they can carry on their business by ordinary methods from this time forth. Unless the Government can bring . forward some bet-
ter policy than it has yet brought forth, these enterprises are on the hands of the country; we have no choice in the matter, and to ask us to vote $23,000,000 now to put into broken-backed enterprises, as they are labelled on both sides of the House, is only putting $23,000,000 out of the power of the people of Canada when it should not be put out of their power. If we are to take over these railroads, now is the time to do so. That seems to be the only conclusion at present. I do not wish to be understood as agreeing that that is the best policy; but in view of the conditions into which the Government has permitted the matter to drift, and in view of the fact that they have no definite proposition to offer for a solution of the problem, there is no need of any commission of inquiry to find out what must be the result.

Will the Minister of Finance state what the policy of the Government will be after this loan is granted, and as I expect it will be granted, as to the Canadian Northern branching out into new fields altogether such as they propose to do in Ontario and which will add greatly to their liabilities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am speaking from memory, but I think, under the legislation of 1914, there is some limitation upon the power of extensions unless with the consent of the Governor in Council. It is the financing of the Canadian Northern that gives immediate concern and that makes this loan necessary. I do not think my hon. friend need be very apprehensive about any extensions of the Canadian Northern-did I understand him to say in Ontario?-because any such extensions would have to be financed, and at present my hon. friend knows how difficult it is to finance.

The minister must be
aware of the campaign that went on for two months of this session in the Railway Committee and in this House to get authority to revive charters to build lines in Ontario that would take many, many millions; yet those interested said that they had the money to carry on the work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not familiar with that situation. I understand the reference is to two electric lines proposed in Ontario. They are part of the Canadian Northern, and if the subsidiary companies concerned are able to finance their enterprises, it will increase the earnings of the

company and will not diminish the security of the Government, hut will rather enhance that security. I speak with incomplete knowledge, for, though it may seem strange to my hon. friend, I am not familiar with the Canadian Northern legislation that is before the House. I accept what the hon. gentleman says-that they have the money for the completion of these lines. But there is nothing in that situation that would immediately connect with the proposal now before the committee, as near as I can see.

The Canadian Northern
enterprise seems to be completed except that part from Capreol to Montreal. What is the intention or expectation with regard to that portion of the scheme as the result of the loan proposed? Capreol is north of Sudbury and is the point of junction between the Montreal branch and the Toronto branch. I understand that the section from Ottawa to Capreol is being operated with local trains, but that on the line from Ottawa to Montreal no trains are being run. It is quite plain that the Canadian Northern cannot be a profitable and completed enterprise as a transcontinental line unless and until that connection is finished. Has this aid in view the securing of the completion of that part of the enterprise?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no doubt they will complete it as soon as they have the financial strength to do so. But this money is not for that immediate purpose; it is to assist them in the situation in which they find themselves in regard to existing obligations for construction and for payment of interest upon securities.

Is it not usual for a financial institution, when dealing with a concern in difficulties, to take into consideration how soon and under what circumstances that concern is going to get into a profitable and earning position? This Canadian Northern, considered as a transcontinental line, is not a completed enterprise. It cannot be made profitable-no one can expect it to be profitable-unless this section of the line is completed and the road put in full operation. Surely, that is a matter for the consideration of the Government when they are giving aid of $15,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If matters of this kind were to be taken into consideration, as I said the other day, instead of $15,000,000 we should have to give them
more. This is the same case as that of the extensions in the West to which my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) referred the other day. We could give them a minimum of aid to carry them during the present year, looking as I have said, to a permanent solution of the question through the investigation that is to be held. The Canadian Northern officials are well aware of the necessity of completing their transcontinental line as early as possible, and they will endeavour to finance the completion of it, if what the hon. gentleman states is correct, and I do not question his view of it.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
To provide for inquiry and report upon the railway situation of Canada, $150,000.

I was not here when the resolution for the Canadian Northern railway was passed, and, with your permission, Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a word or two with regard to it. When these resolutions were first introduced I had made up my mind very distinctly that the only thing to do with the Canadian Northern was'to put it into the hands of a receiver. It was necessary, I thought, to find out just what constituted the Canadian Northern in its various branches, and to keep track of the receipts. As to this loan, I have no doubt that the minister will see that the proceeds are devoted to the purpose for which they are intended. In Speaking of receipts, I refer more particularly to the general receipts for freight and passenger traffic, etc. I was strongly in favour of the appointment of a receiver for this road, because in that way we could keep close track of what is done with those receipts. The Canadian Northern resolution contains the words " such mortgages to contain such terms and conditions as the Governor in Council may approve." It is possible that under that provision the Minister of Finance may be able to appoint someone to have charge of receipts and disbursements. There is a good deal of feeling in the country, whether rightly or wrongly I am not prepared to say, .that the receipts from the railway are not used entirely for the purposes of the railway. I am not as much afraid of the credit of the country being injured by the appointment of a receiver as some people appear to be. However, this is a very serious time so far as finances are concerned, and it is just

possible that the appointment of a receiver for a railway the size of the Canadian Northern might be detrimental to the credit of the country. This being the case, no doubt the difficulty in connection with keeping track of the operation of the railway and knowing exactly its merits and demerits will be overcome by the operations of the commission that the minister proposes to appoint. This will be done, of course, only if the men selected are competent for the position and have an exact knowledge of the conditions affecting the railways throughout this country. As to Government ownership, it is quite possible that through the improvements that may take place in the management of Government railways, we shall be in a position at some time to take over and nationalise the railways, but I do not think that we are in any such position now. The history of the management of Government railways in the past is not such as to encourage us to take on more railways. Last year, according to railway statistics, the proportion of expenses to receipts of privately-owned or corporation-owned railways, including the Canadian Northern, was a little over 72, and of Government railways a little over 102. That would not encourage me by any means to vote for the acquirement and operation of all the railways under Government control. Besides, if the Minister of Finance should have to go to New York or to England or to Europe for money, I do not believe he would get any, because the financiers of this continent, as well as those on the other side of the water, know to a nicety what the cost of the operation of Government railways is in this country, just as they know the cost of the operation of privately-owned or corporation-owned railways. Certainly it would be no inducement to financiers to loan money to Canada in this time of stress if Canada were to pile on top of her present debt, and the debt that has to be incurred during the coming year, the sum of two and a half or three billion dollars for the purchase of these railways. It is possible that time will rectify that condition. When it does, I shall be perfectly willing to see the railways nationalized, but until that time I am not so willing. When I first read these proposals, I was strongly in favour of having the whole of the capital stock of the Canadian Northern assigned to the Government-not handed over to the Government for ownership, but handed over in trust to be handed back when the present operators 
succeed in paying their liability to the Government. I was in favour of that suggestion in 1914, if I mistake not, but after the minister's explanation this afternoon as to the position of the Government in the matter of taking over the railway in case of default-and they are at present in default-and in view of the fact that this is a demand loan, I am not so .much in favour of that proposal now as I was. For the reason which I have given,, I am not so strongly urgent upon a receivership, because, as the minister has pointed out, it is possible that to place this road in the hands of a receiver would injure the credit of the country. If, then, we are not going to take the railways over or put them into the hands of a receiver, the next best thing-probably the best thing-is to appoint this commission, provided they are qualified for the work. As the hon. member for Calgary said this afternoon, in a year from now we ought to be in a position to know just exactly what Ve should do with regard to the railway situation in Canada. It should be discussed, I think, entirely from a non-partisan standpoint ; there is no necessity to enter into recriminations or reflections of any kind in dealing with it. The railway situation is here, and we have got to face it. I personally am not at all despondent over the railway situation, and I think that the members of this House, when they have the exact facts before them, will be quite capable of dealing with that situation in the same manner as a Board of Directors would deal with it, without any recriminations or any partisanship, and in a manner that will be in the best interests of the country. ,

I should like to know why it is that, when the Government are operating the Transcontinental railway and the Canadian Northern railway are operating their own road, the Transcontinental, instead of operating trains between Winnipeg and Quebec, which is the proper eastern terminus of the Transcontinental, operate their trains from Toronto to Winnipeg in competition with the first-class service of the Canadian Pacific railway and also the Canadian Northern railway. Running trains there, the National Transcontinental must run over 500 miles of line which is either leased or operated under running rights. They operate in competition with the Canadian Northern to the disadvantage of both the National Transcontinental railway and the Canadian Northern.

The Acting Minister of Railways the other day made the announcement that on the 1st of June a direct first-class passenger service would be inaugurated between St. John, Halifax and Winnipeg, over the National Transcontinental railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has drawn attention more than once to the exports of the past year. Without desiring to prolong the discussion, I wish to bring to his attention some very striking figures to show the extraordinary efforts that have been put forth, and	successfully	put forth, in
connection with the export business of Canada.	I looked it up and was
surprised to find that Canada during the past year had done so well. For the 11 months ended February, 1915, the grain, wheat and flour exported from Canada amounted to 90,000,000 bushels, whereas foT the 11 months ended February, 1916, the export of grain, wheat and flour amounted to 180,000,000 bushels, just twice as much. So that for the 11 months ended February, 1916, twice as much grain, wheat and flour was exported from Canada as for the 11 months ending in 1915. There is another curious feature in connection with our export business for the same period. Whereas, for the 11 months ending February, 1915,
36.000.	000 of foreign produce, grain, wheat and flour, were exported from Canada, for the 11 months ended February, 1916, only
11.000.	000 were exported. So, while the exports of grain, wheat and flour of Canadian produce were doulbled, the amount of American produce of the like kind exported from Canada fell from 36,000,000 bushels to 11,000,000 bushels. Then, dealing with totals, I find that the total exports for the 11 months in question in each of the years mentioned were 127,000,000 bushels of both Canadian and foreign produce of grain, wiheat and flour, whereas for the 11 months ended February, 1916, no less than 191,000,000 bushels were exported. So we have the extraordinary fact before us that in this year the exports from Canada are enormously in excess of the exports of any other year. I am not saying that this is not as it should be; I am drawing attention to these very striking figures to show that, notwithstanding the shortage of tonnage upon the Atlantic, Canada had been able to increase her exports to such an extraordinary degree as is shown by these figures.

The figures are certainly
very striking and very satisfactory. As figures they are most interesting; but when you say that you say it all, because the fact remains that at the beginning of this month there was, according to the latest returns,
125,000,000 bushels of surplus export grain west of the lakes, and that because of that surplus of grain being west of the Great Lakes at the beginning of this month the people of the West are not able to increase their acreage this season as they would have done if they had been able to dispose of it. As they are not able to increase their acre-_ age, the country does not offer the same attraction to immigration that it would have offered if the acreage could have been increased. My hon. friends on both sides this afternoon were agreed that the question of securing productive occupation of the prairie was the great problem, and they had various ideas as to how it could be solved. I will give a solution of it. If they will secure for the man who now has produced the grain the prompt sale of that grain and a fair price for it, they will then have an effective immigration policy. But they can print all the beautiful literature they please at whatever expense they like, and say what they please in it, and put as many pictures into it as they choose. So long as a man hauls his grain 15 miles to the elevator in the month of May, after he has harvested, and cannot sell it because the elevator is full, and the elevatbr is full because the railroad did not take the grain away, and because of the embargo put on the transportation of grain by the railway companies, for one reason or another-you cannot argue against such a state of facts as that, and you cannot get the people to come and settle in this country in the hope of developing it when, on the evidence of their senses, they cannot sell the grain they have produced. This is absolutely pertinent to the question. 1 do not care how much we have exported. We are being asked to finance these two railroads on the plea that we had overbuilt our railroads and did not have traffic to make them profitable enterprises, while the condition is that we have the traffic and it has not been handled. The answer to that is not given by telling us how much we did, when there is so much that we did not do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think that my hon. friend is scarcely fair in his statement, because he has overlooked the salient fact that the crop of last year in the West was really two crops in one. Our railway

ii- -

system was designed to take care of a certain normal situation. Of course that situation was likely to increase. Last year the West was blessed with two crops in one, and I think it is not an extraordinary fact-although nobody would be more desirous than I to see the crop moved out quickly- that the whole of the crop of last year has not yet been taken out. Personally, I would be very much pleased if it had been taken out, but we all know that the railway companies could not take out a double crop with machinery that might have been perfectly capable of taking out a normal crop, or even a crop considerably in excess of the normal. They had to deal this year with a double crop situation in the West, and I thought that my hon. friend would be interested in seeing the figures which I produced for the information of the committee, because they show that the export of our wheat and wheat flour was twice as large during the 11 months ending February of this year as it was for the same period of the previous year. While we have not been able to meet the situation in its entirety, I cannot help thinking that, having regard to the scarcity of tonnage which has prevailed upon the Atlantic, it is a very notable record which I have exhibited to the committee.

There is no question that it is a very creditable record, but it is not creditable enough. That is not the point. The point I wish to insist upon is that here we are dealing with what is said to be a desperate situation, which exists for lack of traffic, while the fact is that we have the traffic which we have not handled in the time in which it ought to be handled. That is a situation which the Government has not risen to meet. We are told that we have too many railroads, and the evidence is that we have not handled the products which we had on hand, and which ought to be handled in order to make our business a success. The two conditions of fact do not meet at all. There must be mishandling or mismanagement somewhere, for which our friends who are in control of the affairs of the country must accept their full measure of responsibility.
Another point is that in the statement of exports of Canadian grain-I presume my hon. friend has the figures-I think something like 70 or 75 per cent of our exports of last season's crop went by way of the United States, and only the balance went through Canadian ports. The share of the cro-p that went to Buffalo went by lake

transportation. We have three lines of railways running from the prairies to the sea, and every bushel of grain that finds an outlet over the lakes was a bushel of grain taken away from the possible traffic on one or other of these three lines of railway. When we have the condition that we have to-day, our railways bankrupt for lack of traffic, and our traffic going in such an enormous proportion to the United States, instead of to our own ports, 1 repeat it is for the Government to make the explanation, and the explanation cannot be made on the basis of a capable and competent management of the affairs of this country.

It is now half-past eight, and we have just been handed a mass of documents relating to the Quebec and Saguenay proposition, which, we are told, is to be taken up to-night. It is the first information we have had concerning it, and I just want to say, for the benefit of the Minister of Railways, that it is showing scant courtesy to the House. It is impossible for those who asked for this information to digest it in the time allowed; perhaps they were not expected to have time to digest it.
With regard to this other item, it would have been better, to my mind, if the Government had been able to give us the names of the three commissioners, for the simple reason that the experience of us all is, first, that the work of a commission largely depends upon the calibre of the men who compose it. If the Government cannot give us the names of these men, I think it ought to have given us a copy of the instructions which it proposes to place in the hands of the commissioners. We all know that, no matter what the subject may be, or what the calibre of the men forming a commission may be, their work depends on the powers which are given to them. This commission might he composed of the best men that could be secured in the world, and their report might not be worth five cents to the people of Canada. The Government will say: You can trust us to give them full scope. I am not going to say that Parliament cannot trust the Government, but men have different ideas even as to the meaning of language. What those of us Who are not of the legal profession might think was a pretty wide latitude, legal gentlemen might regard as no latitude at all, or longitude either. The commissioners are thus tied up in a box, and can only move a few inches each way. I think

it would have been more satisfactory if the Government had been able to give us a copy of the instructions in the identical language in which they propose to confer certain powers upon this commission, so that every member of this House could judge what the commission intended to do, and how far it could go. The value of the report will depend on the wording of these instructions. Presuming the commission is not armed with as wide powers as it ought to have, it is not stretching one's imagination to think that it might go to the offices of one of the railway companies and be refused certain information which Parliament might desire it to have.
