The commission might be in quest of some practical information, such as the experience of certain other roads or of financiers; and unless they were given the fullest possible powers, and those powers were clearly defined, they might be unable to get that information for us. I make that suggestion to. the minister, and I do not think it would be a very difficult one to carry out. If the Government has in mind just what powers they propose to give to tfiis commission, a discussion for an hour or so, in which we would be able to give our ideas, might put the matter in even better shape.
There is another matter to which I wish to call attention, particularly the attention of the Minister of Finance. I submit that this committee has a right to have placed before it an estimate of the cost of operation of the National Transcontinental for the year. I know I shall be told that there is a statute. But that statute was not designed to cover the enlarged operation now proposed. The House should know what money the Government proposes to expend, so that we could discuss the proposition of the Government intelligently. Every year an amount is put in the Estimates for the Intercolonial, and we discuss it thoroughly, perhaps too thoroughly sometimes; but at all events the rights of the members of Parliament are preserved to them when they have the opportunity of discussing expenditures in that way. When the operation was only on a small scale there was perhaps not so much objection to the Government not submitting estimates, but now that the Government has taken over the Transcontinental and proposes to expend millions in operation each year, it is unfair to the House not to submit an estimate. We should be given the opportunity of discussing what is to be done with the money
251*
and the question of operation; and then when the report comes in at the end of the year hon. gentlemen would be able to see whether their directions in regard to the expenditure of the money had been properly carried out.

I was not in the House when the hon. gentleman rose to speak, but I have been told that he stated that the documents relating to the Bill I have on the Order Paper were not given to the House until 8 or 8.30 this evening.
I said they came to the House at 8 or 8.30.

And the hon. gentleman considered that I had treated him with scant courtesy. I think it is hardly fair for him to say that, because he was sitting in the House this afternoon at two o'clock when I handed in the documents that are now before him, and I think he must have heard me say that I was laying them on the Table.
I did not hear anything of the kind.

The hon. gentleman was in the House at the time, and surely he can not censure me for not having heard what I said. As soon as the Orders of the Day were called, I handed in the papers, and I took it for granted that he heard what I said. A few minutes afterwards I thought I saw the hon. member reading them, but that turns out not to be the fact. I do not think I could have done anything more. I was unable to get the papers at an earlier date. The hon. gentleman walked out of the House shortly after I handed in the papers, and I thought he was reading them. Under the circumstances I think it was hardly fair for him to accuse me of discourtesy. With regard to my hon. friend's suggestion that we should give an estimate of the proposed expenditure on the National Transcontinental, it is quite true, as he says, that a certain amount is placed in the Estimates for the Intercolonial every year. But the Intercolonial was built fifty or sixty years ago, and has been in operation for many years. On the other hand, we have only been operating the Transcontinental for eight or ten months, and it is not fair to ask us to put in an estimate of what it will cost until we have been operating the road a little longer. No man living can give an approximate estimate of the cost of operating the Transcontinental during the coming year. Surely

we should (be allowed to operate the road for one year in order to get an idea of what it will cost before being asked to submit an estimate to Parliament. At the end of the fiscal year, on March 31st last, when we had been operating the road for only eight months, how could we tell what a year's operation would cost?
Add a third of a year's expenses to the amount spent at the end of eight months.

We want to run the road for a year and see what it will cost, and then next year we shall 'be able to submit a statement to the House, and there is no doubt that an amount will be put in the Estimates for the Transcontinental, and that the road will be treated in that Te-spect just the same as the Intercolonial and other railways operated by the Government. I submit that it is only fair that we should be allowed to run the Transcontinental for one yeaT before being asked to submit an estimate. There is no other reason than that why an estimate should not be given.

I am sorry there is a misunderstanding between the minister and myself. I regret I did not hear what he said this afternoon. I never repeat private conversations, and I am not going "to now, but I understood the minister was going to send me the documents at ten minutes to two; I was told so by a gentleman. I stayed in all afternoon waiting for them. They were not discovered until 8.20 in the Clerk's office. What the minister says about the Transcontinental is loud, but not strong, and for this reason: the Government should not segregate itself from Parliament. It is not the Government that is running this railway, but Parliament, and hon. members are just as much interested in it as is the Government, and have a right to know what the Government propose to do, so far as the Government can tell them. The manager can surely give an approximate estimate of what he proposes to do on the Transcontinental this year; that is always done in the case of the Intercolonial. It is true there is never a year but what he comes back for $1,000,000 or $2,000,000 more. It depends on the traffic; if the traffic is heavy expenses are greater, and if the traffic is light the expenses are less. That is to be expected in the case of enterprises where it is impossible to give a very

close estimate. I am not charging the minister with any wrong-doing in holding back this estimate, but what I am saying is that as we are taking the Transcontinental over as a business proposition the manager should give an approximate estimate of what amount will be needed for the year. When hon. members go home to their constituencies they will be asked: " What is it going to cost to operate the Transcontinental? I see you are taking it over." and we shall have to tell them that an estimate was never given to' the House. The point I am making is that the Government is taking to itself authority which the Parliament never intended it should have, for it was never thought that the Government would operate the Irancontinental permanently. I say the Government should submit an estimate of the cost just as in the case of any other public work. But as the minister has said that he will submit an estimate next year, I will not say anything further on that point. If the road is to be permanently operated by the Government the appropriation ought to be asked for in the usual way.

How does the minister
propose to get the money for the operation of this road if he does not put an item in the Estimates?	*

.Under the Act, all the expenses of operation can be taken out of the Consolidated Fund. The desire of the Government is td get that money in the same way as we got the money for the operation of the Intercolonial. We are waiting until we get out organization complete. We have not the train service thoroughly organized on the Transcontinental between Moncton and Winnipeg, but when we get out power and our cars so that we can give the system a fair trial, we shall know what the road will cost. As soon as we are in a position to make a proper estimate of the cost of operation of'the Transcontinental, that will be placed in the Estimates in the usual way, but it must be borne in mind that the road was taken over only last July. The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) states that we know what it is costing from Toronto to Winnipeg, and if we ask him what it is costing to operate the Transcontinental between Toronto and Winnipeg he can give us the figures. If he wants the figures for the cost of operation between Cochrane and Moncton or any other portion of the Transcontinental up to the present time, I will telegraph and get them

for him, because there is no desire to keep the figures secret. As soon as it is possible for the Kailway Department as a whole to get the Transcontinental into the same position as the Intercolonial, so that we can come to Parliament and say: Our estimate for the operation of the Transcontinental is so and so, that will and must be done, no matter who is in charge of the Railway Department.

Will the minister tell us
what the Government proposes to do in the way of improving the service between Cochrane and Quebec? The minister must know that since the operation of the road was started that service has been most unsatisfactory and unfair to the people of that district.

Probalbly the hon. gentleman was not here the other evening when this matter came up. The operation between Cochrane and Quebec has since it was started been a local service. We had neither the equipment nor the organization complete. I stated here the other evening that there will be a through service from Halifax and St .John to Winnipeg commencing, we expect, about the first of June. Of course, you cross at Quebec. Up to the present time the arrangement has been that we run three days a week and the Canadian Northern run the other three days. It is our intention to have a through passenger train that will go right on from Quebec to Winnipeg.
Daily?

I do not think it will be a daily service to start with. We will run it in connection with the train from Tor-, onto, the two meeting at Cochrane, and the train will go right through. We will, of course, put on whatever service is necessary.

Before this item carries, I want again to impress upon the minister that as soon as possible the Transcontinental should be used as a route for the outlet of the western wheat. There is no doubt that wheat can be carried over that road at t'he summer rate of lake and rail, show a profit, be a big advantage to the grain producer, and give a large amount of freight to the railway. In that way we would take a great deal more of our grain to our own ports. This last year, about 75 per cent of our crop went to American ports, and with the summer rate that the Government has put in force, there is an opportunity of furnishing freight and work for the Government railroads, cutting down the loss, if there is going to be a loss, in operating them, and of operating the roads to the advantage of all concerned. I trust the minister will give the matter his best attention as soon as he can get sufficient rolling stock.

I certainly agree with the
hon. member that we should operate the Transcontinental as much as possible. What is surprising me at the present time is this. Our rate from Armstrong to Quebec is six cents and I understand that the rate from Winnipeg to Armstrong is six cents. I have not made inquiries of late but I am informed that the lake and rail rate from Montreal to Port Arthur is nine cents. Therefore, wheat shipped from the West all rail through to Quebec should get to Quebec for about three cents less than if shipped via Port Arthur, lake and rail, to Montreal. I do not know whether that is the way it works out or not, but those are the rates in force, and if that is the way it works out, why is not the wheat being shipped all rail to Quebec? I understand there are about 18,000,000 bushels of grain along the Grand Trunk Pacific that has to come east, and I cannot understand why that grain is not sent over the Transcontinental to Quebec, instead of via Port Arthur to Montreal. Perhaps my hon. friends from the West will make inquiries as to the situation and find out where the trouble lies, because our six cent rate from Armstrong which is on the same line as Fort William, is still in force, and wheat shipped via Armstrong goes right down to Quebec instead of going to Montreal.

One explanation may be
that perhaps there is not vessel space at Quebec to take away the grain as fast as it will come in, the minister must also not forget that this six cent rate' is not in force to Montreal where there is the largest milling capacity in Canada, and a great deal of the wheat going out by vessel from Fort William and Port Arthur to Montreal is perhaps consigned to the large millers in Montreal for export.

As those vessels take full
cargoes of wheat, they can take it just as well at Quebec as at Montreal. At all events some grain should be going to Quebec where we have an elevator capacity of one and a half to one and three-quarter million bushels, and yet there is no wheat going that way. If there is that difference of

three cents in the rate, the wheat should go that way, because the vesels can be got at Quebec just as well as at Montreal.

I think this is a question for an energetic Minister of Railways who will attend to business, do some advertising -and send two or three men over the Grand Trunk Pacific to point out to the shippers the advantage of shipping to Quebec. The shippers are accustomed to shipping via lake and rail and they may not know of the advantage to be gained by shipping by this route. Therefore, instead of depending upon outsiders, I think the acting minister should take the matter up himself.

I have advertised this rate
pretty well this session and it should be known in the West.

The minister is going
in the right direction, but it is a good plan not to depend upon others for what you can do yourself.
Will any member of the Government condescend to reply to my suggestion as to the powers to be given to the commissioners?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
thought we might have explained the terms of the commission which we purpose to issue. The terms of that commission have not been settled, but I stated in general words what we had in view, namely, that full report should be made upon the
9 p.m. physical and financial condition of the railways of Canada and upon the general railway situation, in order that we might be in a position to adopt a policy which would prevent these recurring -visits for temporary aid, and settle the railway situation in permanent fashion. The powers which will be given to the commission will have to receive careful consideration on the part of the Government in order that that end which we have in view will be accomplished. I am not able to present the wording of the commission which will be issued, because its terms have not yet been settled, but it seems to me that it is only a matter of language apt to clothe the commissioners with the powers to obtain for us the information which we desire for the purpose which we have in view. I stated in introducing these loan proposals to the House that we not only desired the information which we thought a commission could furnish us respecting the physical and financial conditions of the

railways and railway companies of Canada, but that we hoped to obtain from the commission suggestion and advice as to what distribution or rearrangement or linking up of lines and systems would give the best economic result for the enormous amount of capital which had been expended upon the railways of Canada. We have in mind a commission clothed with wide powers which will bring in a comprehensive report, as a result of which we shall know what policy, at least in our view, should be adopted to settle, as I have said, in permanent fashion this railway situation with which we are confronted. This problem cannot be side-stepped or escaped. This loan proposal is a measure of temporary assistance, and if the action which we propose to take were not taken, in all probability at the next session of the House, and possibly at the next after that, we might be confronted with a similar situation to that which confronts us to-day. There is every reason, therefore, why the Government should seek a permanent solution, and obtain the best advice which it possibly can get from the ablest experts available for the purpose in order that it may solve the problem which is presenting itself at recurring intervals and which demands solution.
The personnel of the commission has not yet been settled by the Government. The suggestion is put forward that the Government should be ready with the names of the members of the commission. I need not say that it is not an easy task to settle upon the names of men of the ability and of the impartial judgment which will be required to investigate the railway situation of Canada. Some hon. gentlemen have said that we should find these men in Canada; others suggest that they should be found in the United States. Undoubtedly there will be a difficulty in finding them in Canada, for the reason-speaking only for myself-that it would not he easy to find competent men in this country not connected with the existing railway situation and who could bring impartial judgment to bear upon the matter. The railways are competitors one with the other. It is possible that one or more of the men may be found in Canada, but whether found in Canada or in the United States, my own view is that they should be men of eminent ability and of such standing that they will command the confidence of the public, men who will deal with the matter without bias, without prejudice, unin-

fluenced by any interest in the existing situation. To the problem of finding those men the Government must address itself. We have not fixed on three as the number. We stated that we would appoint three directors upon t'he board of the Canadian Northern Railway Company and three directors upon the board of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. I may say that it is not the intention of the Government to appoint so-called dummy directors, as has been suggested this afternoon, as representatives of the Government upon the boards of these two railways. We shall endeavour to find outstanding men who have the interests of the Government at heart and who will command the confidence of the people of Canada. The suggestion has been put forward during the progress of this discussion that there should be an audit of the revenues -and expenditures of the Canadian Northern. It was not suggested that there should be a similar audit of the revenues and expenditures of the Grand Trunk Pacific, but the two lines stand on the same footing and there is just as much reason for the one as for the other. We have provided for that. We have an estimate of $10,000 for the purpose of retaining and paying two firms of auditors for carrying on a continuous audit, beginning May 1, of the revenues and expenditures of the Canadian Northern Railway Company and of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. We feel that by reason of the guarantees and loans which we have made to these two railways we have a very vital interest in the conduct of their business from this time forward, or at all events until they are in such position that they will no longer need Government aid, if such a condition ever arises. It is our intention to appoint firms of auditors of very high standing who will command the confidence of the people. As it has been suggested that the net profits of the Canadian Northern railway system may have been diverted for other than railway purposes, I would call the attention of the committee to this fact,-because I do not believe that any hon. member desires to do any injustice to the Canadian Northern railway management-that the accounts of that company which have been laid before the House are audited by -an eminent Winnipeg firm of very high standing, Messrs. Webb, Read and Hegan, chartered accountants. Personally I see no reason to believe that the net earnings of the Canadian
Northern Railway Company have been used for any other purpose than the purposes of the railway; in fact, that is borne out by the statement that we have before us. For the fiscal year 1915, which ended on .Tune 30 of last year, there was a net profit of $6,000,000 and for the present year there is an estimated net profit of $9,700,000. The net profits of that road have not been diverted to other than railway purposes. We can see where they have gone. The net profits, that is to say the amount of revenue in excess of operating expenses have gone, generally speaking, to two purposes. They have gone to pay interest upon underlying securities, that is to say, fixed charges; or they have gone to pay indebtedness incurred or expenditure made upon construction, or for the payment oi instalments of equipment securities. There is an indebtedness, as I pointed out to the committee, in respect of those items, but the net earnings of the company so far as they went unquestionably were applied to that purpose.
As I stated, you have first the report of the administration of the Canadian Northern itself, and then you have the certificate of a very reputable firm of auditors in Winnipeg. In addition to that, we propose to appoint three directors upon the board of the Canadian Northern and three upon the board of the Grand Trunk Pacific, to keep the Government informed as to the administration of these railways. We propose, also, that there shall be an audit of the expenditures and revenues of each company on behalf of the Government, and it is our intention to name in this connection auditors who will command the confidence of the Canadian* public.

The minister has brought up another point. I thought it had been decided that there were to be three commissioners, but apparently the Government does not know whether there are to be three or more than three.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I never mentioned any limitation of the number of commissioners to be appointed; there may be three or more than three, as the Government shall decide.

No chance of having
less than three?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For myself, I think there should be at least three.

At the rate the Government are going in appointing directors and

commissioners they will hardly find applicants enough possibly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, you know we have a population of eight millions.
But you must not interfere too much with recruiting, you know.

The newspapers announced that there were to be three commissioners and how they were to be appointed; the Government to appoint two, one a financier, and the other a railway man,, and these two to appoint a third. I discussed that the other night. But, to come back to the other point: Will this commission be instructed to report and make recommendations, and will the Government feel that it is bound to accept the recommendations they make? Or will they be asked to report, as the lawyers say, the evidence, and not make recommendations ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They will be
asked to advise generally as to the railway situation >and to report as to what arrangement, distribution, or linking up of the lines or systems will give the best economic results. We cannot make any commission a dictator; we cannot abdicate the functions of the Government or of Parliament in favour of any commission. But we hope the coznmission will give us the benefit of expert knowledge to enable us to find a permanent solution of the railway situation. Speaking for myself, I should think it extremely inexpedient that the Government should devolve upon the commission the powers of Parliament. Obtaining expert advice is one thing, but whether the Government and Parliament should accept that advice is another. I do not think we should fetter ourselves in advance.

As to conferring upon a commis.iion the powers of Government, the hon. minister has forgotten that, only two or mree weexs ago, at the instance of the Government, our function in regard to railway charters were turned over to the Railway Commission. But I leave that aside. The appointment of this commission is of vast importance. It seems to me that it would be better to take whatever amount of money the Government intends to spend in the salaries of these commissioners, and spend it in getting say two men, one man to deal with the physical conditions of the railways, and how they can best be worked for the general advantage of the people,

and the other to look into the finances of the road. Or, instead of appointing three men at comparatively large salaries, get the best man you can find in America and give him the salary you would pay to the three. If you were to do this, I believe you would have a report that would be worth ten times as much as one made by three men. If you have three men on a commission, the work is done by the best man of the three-he practically decides the whole business. As to the gathering of information, that is a matter for clerical and other assistance. I should be in favour of a small commission.

That is part of what I had in mind. The minister will notice that the newspapers are giving him advice as to the personnel of this commission. He has been advised not to neglect to have as one member of the commission a man who is in favour of Government ownership. Another portion of the press tell him that the report will be incomplete unless he has a labour representative on the commission. There are two distinct lines of advice that I have particularly noticed. If suggestions and recommendations are to be asked by this commission, in addition to an investigation of facts, it will be all the more necessary to be very, very careful as to the personnel. If it were possible to have all shades of opinion on the commission, it would be very well; but that might easily make the commission top heavy.
How many does the hon. member suggest as the membership of this commission?

I would not have more than three at the outside. I have tried commissions, and I have found that the larger the commission the more trouble you have in arriving at a conclusion. As the hon. member for Assiniboia has said, the acquiring of technical information does not need a commission; the commissioners should be able men who can digest the information when they get it. I do not think I will say more on the subject. The Government has my views. I would merely urge that the instructions to be given to the commission should first be drafted and then thought over for several days, and looked at in the light of full and mature consideration. Upon the powers given to the commission will depend the usefulness of their work.

I do not know whether the minister will attach much importance

to my knowledge of railway matters, but I would like to give, not only to the Minister of Railways but to his colleagues, my idea on this subject. I think there is danger in making the mistake of not developing talent in our departments by going all over the country looking for commissioners. I think that the proper policy would be to employ big men in the various departments of the Government-and big men are needed in every department-pay them large salaries if necessary, and place responsibility upon them. That would be very much better than going outside when any big question arises and employing men at high salaries, perhaps to learn the business in hand at the expense of the Government, and then to leave the service of the Government. By having men of ability permanently employed in the departments they would be constantly at hand to give the Government the benefit of their advice and assistance in carrying out the recommendations which they might make, whereas outside commissioners, when employed in this way, are of no further use to the Government after they have made their report. The Government employs a general manager of the Government railways at a salary of $20,000 per annum. He is, I believe, a thoroughly competent man,- if he is not he is not capable of earning this salary,-and the Government will not be able to secure better advice than he should be able to give by the employment of any outside commission. There is the further fact that when a report is made by the outside commissioners, who may he employed, the officers of the department may say: If you had consulted us in the first place we could have given you better advice than you have received; the plan that has been recommended to you is of no use. The practice of employing outside men to do responsible work in the departments is not a good one. We see it constantly in the Justice department. Not long ago when a little Bill was to be drafted we had lawyers from Halifax, Quebec and Vancouver gathered here to draft it.
What Bill does the hon. gentleman refer to?

It was a Bill in connection with the war laws. A few days ago a man was added to the Department of Justice, which of course was carrying out the idea I suggest, and I think is the proper course. We should not have lawyers gathering around, like crows around a carcase whenever there is any legislation to be drafted.
As - to the nationalization of railways, I am opposed to it. I believe that we should encourage individual energy, enterprise and initiative instead of putting everything into a common pool, which tends to kill individual enterprise. We should take a leaf out of the book of the United States, where there has been little nationalization. The United States have developed to their piresent greatness through individual effort and enterprise.
To provide for a continuous audit on behalf of the Government of Canada, commencing May 1st, 1916, of the revenues and expenditures of the Canadian Northern railway and Grand Trunk Pacific railway systems, $10,000.
This is apparently carrying out what I was suggesting, having an audit of the receipts and disbursements. I did not know, when I made my remarks, that this item was in the Estimates.

There are two questions in connection with the Canadian Northern railway which I think might well be considered at this juncture. One is in connection with the Hudson Bay railway. The Government-owned section of the road runs from the Saskatchewan river to Hudson bay, and is connected with the railway system of the Northwest, through the Canadian Northern main line at Prince Albert, by a branch line, 90 miles in length. The'sole ownership of that branch lies in the Canadian Northern railway. It would seem desirable that, if the Hudson Bay road is to be operated as a Government proposition, it should ultimately be extended southwesterly as far as Regina or Moosejaw; but for the time being there would be an immediate advantage in the ownership of the branch connection from Hudson Bay Junction to the Pas. I think it wise to go on record now as suggesting that that would be a proper matter to be taken under consideration and dealt with, because it will probably have to be done at some time, and this would seem to be as appropriate a time as any to make the arrangement.
Another suggestion has been made by the Quebec Board of Trade; that is, that access for the Transcontinental into Montreal should be secured over the Canadian Northern railway branch from Montreal to Harvey Junction.
That is 116 miles.

It seems that the mileage from Winnipeg to Montreal is something

less by that Toute than by Cochrane, North Bay and Scotia Junction, while of course the traffic ie hauled over the rails of the Transcontinental for a very much longer distance, and the grade is good all the way into Montreal. I do not know whether these points have been suggested to the minister, or have come to his attention, or whether he has any views on the subject. It would seem to me that, in dealing with the Canadian Northern, this would be a suitable time to make arrangements with the- Canadian Northern for the future to acquire permanent rights over these two pieces of railroad.

The suggestions are good. With reference to the Hudson Bay connection, the hon. member knows that it will be a year or so before that road is out of the hands of the contractors. The commission which is to go to work almost at once will no doubt consider the whole railway situation, as it concerns the West, as well as other parts of Canada, and no doubt they will take up that point in their investigation. With regard to the connection between Hervey Junction and Montreal, that matter has come before me. * The suggestion is a good one, and is being taken up with the view of making the connection, so far as Montreal is concerned. There is no trouble in making arrangements of that kind. We can arrange it satisfactorily either by consulting together, or through the Board of Railway Commissioners. The advantage would be that we would be able to take the whole trainload over the Transcontinental, with the exception of a stretch of about 106 or 116 miles, and where you are dealing with a six cent rate, by bringing it over the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway and then over the Grand Trunk railway, there is very little left for the Transcontinental. As I have said, the suggestion is a good one and is being considered, and it may be taken advantage of before another year. I am in hopes that the whole railway question will be in such a shape next session that we will all be seized of the facts through having the advice of good men who will look into the matter thoroughly.
Progress reported.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.

speechtext:
Hon. J. D. REID (Acting Minister of Railways) moved the second reading of

Bill No. 101, to authorize the acquisition of lines of railway between the city of Quebec and Nairn Falls and between Lyster and St. Jean des Chaillons.
He said: This Bill is for the purpose of acquiring as part of the Government railway system three lines of railway. One is known as the Quebec, Montmorency and Charlevoix railway, extending from St. Paul street in the city of Quebec to St. Joachim, a distance of about 43 1/5 miles. This road has already been in operation for many years.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: In what direction does it run?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: From Quebec, east along the St. Lawrence-that is the electric railway- to St. Anine de Beaupre, and further on. To. Ste. Anne de Beaupre is a distance of about 20 miles, and the railway runs along the St. -Lawrence to the point I have mentioned.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
On the north shore?
* Mr. REID:	On the north shore. As 1
have said, this road has been in operation for many years, and has been a paying proposition for some time.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: They should not sell it then.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
It is a part of the system.
We are also acquiring the Lotbiniere and Megantic railway extending from Lyster in the county of Megantic to St. Jean des Chaillons in the county of Lotbiniere, a distance of about thirty miles. This road has also been in operation for a number of years and is a paying road. The other road we are acquiring is what is known as the Quebec and Saguenay railway, extending from its junction with the Quebec, Montmorency and Charlevoix railway at St. Joachim in the county of Montmorency to Nairn Falls in the county of Charlevoix, a distance of about sixty-two and eight-tenths miles. This road is completed. Nairn Falls is about six miles from Murray Bay, and has some pulp and paper mills.

speechtext: How far is that from the Saguenay river?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
About thirty or forty miles. This road was originally to go to Baie St. Catherines . The object in purchasing the Quebec and Montmorency is to have the road run right into the city of Quebec. The earnings of the Quebec, Montmorency and Charlevoix railway are as follows:
