subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
Do I understand that
this 30 miles cost on an average $91,000 a mile?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: That figure includes the terminals in Quebec, which were very expensive. Then the road is electrified.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Has the minister any reliable reports on these roads?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
We have had our engineers
go over the road, and their reports aTe included in the papers that have been submitted. The cost of the Lotbiniere and Me-gantio railway, which was purchased only two or three years ago, was $285,075.95, plus cost of surveys of line, legal and trust fees, etc., $64,132.70, or a total of $349,208.85. I am giving the statement of cost as it has been given to me.
The Quebec and Saguenay railway was, I understand, incorporated on May 20, 1905, the incorporators being E. D. Garneau, Hon. Charles Langelier, George Tanguay, M.P.P.; Narcisse Rioux, Hon. Alexander Taschereau, William Price, Mark Workman, McLea Walbank and W. G. Ross. That railway extends from the east end of the Quebec and Montmorency road on to Murray bay, the original intention being to go to St. Catherines bay, and making that a winter port. The charter was amended on the 28th day of February, 1907.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Is it a provincial charter or a Dominion charter?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: A Quebec charter. Evidently the work did not begin for some time, because my memorandum shows that construction was begun on the 15th of April, 1911, and the work was stopped in September, 1912.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Construction on the Quebec and Saguenay railway apparently had to cease as soon as reciprocity was defeated.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
The fact that reciprocity was defeated, even supposing it caused the stoppage of this work, was a good thing for the Dominion of Canada. This railway will be revived again, and I hope it will be as successful as the defeat of reciprocity was. About 87 per cent of this railway is finished. The amount that has been expended upon it up to the present time is as follows: The company issued bonds to the extent of $4,684,400. $2,500,000 worth of those bonds were sold at 84 cents on the dollar, and $2,184,400 were sold at 82 cents on the dollar, realising together $3,822,315.42. They have expended all this money and $1,050,000 more in cash, all of which has been put into the road. Therefore they have put into the road $4,872,315.42 of actual cash, and there is due for small claims, a balance for right of way and other accounts, $461,000, making a total of $5,333,315.42, which the company claim has been paid out for the construction of this road so far as it has gone. They received from the Dominion Government in cash at

one, time for subsidies $132,000, which amount was paid to cancel $144,000 worth of the bonds that I have mentioned. Another subsidy, amounting to $116,000, has been deposited with the trust company, and has not yet been paid out to the Quebec and Saguenay railway. Therefore, they have received altogether in subsidies $248,000, but we get back $116,000 of the subsidies so paid, so that the total subsidy that the railway has received is $132,000. I understand that, according to their charter, they were to have received 189,000 acres of land and $3,000 a mile from the Quebec Government, but of that nothing has been given to them up to the present time.
In regard to the condition of the road, at the present time, according to the report of Mr. Beckwith, from Mile 30 to Mile 51 upwards of 95 per cent of the road is finished; from Mile 51 to Mile 56, which is about the heaviest part of the work, 40 per cent is finished; from Mile 56 to Mile 62, 95 per cent of the road is graded; from Mile 62 to Mile 65, there are several unfinished rock cuts, but about 85 per cent of the total work is finished.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend, when he says that the road is finished, mean that the grading is finished, or that the rails have been laid?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: The roadbed has been graded; the ties are there, but the rails are not laid. From Mile 65 to Mile 79 a number of washouts have occurred, but about 85 per cent of the roadbed has been completed, and we have a great many ties to place on this road. From Mile 79 to Mile 81, 6,000 feet of the light work has gone, but otherwise that part is completed; from Mile 81 to Mile 85, 95 per cent of the work has been completed, and from Mile 95 to Nairn falls it is completed. That is the condition of that part of the road from St. Joachim to Nairn falls. There have been several estimates as to what it will cost to finish the road and put it in the condition in which it was when the contractors ceased work. Owing to the road having been left without any work being done on it since 1912, there are a'number of washouts, etc., which must, of course, be repaired.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Will the minister give the estimates of the cost?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: The contractors thought it would cost about $700,000 to complete the road.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: That is to put it in the condition in which it was before?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: To put the road in the condition in which it was before and to lay the rails, making the road all complete and ready for operation.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
There are different
weights of rails along the road-56 and 67 pound rails?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: There are not many rails there, only enough for about eighteen or twenty miles altogether, and those rails are lighter than the ordinary. The reason this railway has cost so much is that it was built to Transcontinental specifications and there was a great deal of hard rock-cut. The cost for reproducing and placing it in condition for operation and completion one contractor estimates at about $700,000. Our engineer who went over the road estimated it at something over $1,000,000.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: What engineer?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: I think his name is Beckwith. In fact two or three engineers of the Intercolonial went over this road. The road was originally proposed to give a service to the people who are living on the north shore. We all know that the people on the south shore are well served with railways, while those living on the north shore have no railway accommodation.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Perhaps the minister will give us information as he goes along. I see by the Bill that the road is 62.8 miles long.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Yes, that is the Quebec and Saguenay.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: How much is completed and open for traffic, and how much unfinished?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: I gave that information at the beginning. Mile 30 is the end of the Quebec and Montmorency and the commencement of the Quebec and Saguenay. From mile 30 to mile 91 is the distance the hon. gentleman mentioned. I stated that from mile 30 to mile 51 the work was upward of ninety-five per cent completed, and according to the statement I have, the road is eighty-seven per cent completed throughout.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
According to the figures as I have taken them down, something over $5,000,000 has been expended on 62-8 miles, of which the grading is only 871 per cent completed, with no rails laid, no sta-

tions built, but, I presume, with the bridges built, although I am not sure as to that. Figure that out, and you will find that this road has cost more than completed railways even in difficult parts of the country. I think it would be advisable for the minister to explain where the money has gone.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
I explained that these are
the figures given me by the Quebec and Saguenay Railway.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Has there been no audit?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
Not by us; but we only agree to pay what it actually cost, up to a certain amount. Perhaps I had better state now what our proposition is, because that will afford me an opportunity to explain an amendment that I shall propose
10 p.m. to this Bill when .we get into committee. The. cost of the Quebec and Montmorency railway, as I stated, was $2,992,209.89. There are bonds on this railway of $2,500,000. We propose, if it is proven to the satisfaction of the Exchequer Court that this money has. actually been spent on the road, to assume the $2,500,000 of bonds for the railroad and the terminals.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: About $70,000 a mile.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: If it cost that. The Exchequer Court must be satisfied that the amount has actually gone into the road.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
Irrespective of whether
it is worth it now or not?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
If it is necessary to have this part of the road in order to have the through road from Quebec to Murray Bay and St. Catherine's bay, if it is extended. By taking this road we can reach Quebec city. That is the reason why we require this piece of road, and, as I have stated, it is a paying road. Now, from St. Joachim to Nairn Falls, according to this statement, they have spent $5,533,315. It is with regard to this that I shall propose an amendment, asked for by Judge Cassels of the Exchequer Court, with a view to making it plainer and providing that he may be able to go thoroughly into the matter. I shall propose to add to the Bill the following words:
Said value to be the actual cost of said railways less depreciation, but not to exceed $4,465,000 exclusive of outstanding bonded indebtedness which is to be assumed by the Government, but not to exceed in all $2,500,000.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: That is on the short piece?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
The short piece is the electric road and steam road, which has been
earning the amounts I have stated. And even if they can show, as they say they can easily show, that they have expended the amount I have stated, the Judge of the Exchequer Court will not be allowed to exceed $4,465,000, but not that amount unless it is shown that much money has been expended on the Quebec and Saguenay, the Lotbin-iere and Megantic, and the Quebec and Montmorency.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: The amendment seems to rather tie the hands of the Judge of the Exchequer Court, because, while it fixes a low valuation, it makes no provision for a reduction on account of the Dominion subsidy which has been paid. If the minister thinks that the cost ought to be considered instead of the value, ought not the subsidy to be deducted?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Of that $132,000 has been paid, and $116,000 has not been paid. We propose that they must show that they have actually expended on the three roads $4,465,000 of cash.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
Will that include in- '
terest on the money that they have invested from year to year?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: What I meant was that if he had regard only to the' amount actually expended, the judge of the Exchequer Court would not be allowed to deduct the $132,000 which has already been paid by the Dominion by way of subsidy.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
I think the subsidy should
be deducted; we can take that up in committee. The Quebec and Saguenay state that they have expended $5,333,315 less the subsidy of $116,000, leaving $5,217,315. Hon. gentlemen can see that if we put in the words " actual cost " without limiting the amount, we would have to pay the $5,300,000. Replying to the hon. member for Guysborough, I may say that during the construction of a road interest is always added to the cost of construction until the road is completed.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: At what rate?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: I do not know what the rate is. I can easily have that information when we are in committee.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: One of these roads, the Quebec and Saguenay, stopped construction in September, 1911.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: It synchronized.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Yes, it synchronized with the defeat of reciprocity. According to what my hon. friend says now, he would propose to pay interest from the time the road began construction up to the present moment.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: No, I said during construction, until the road was completed.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
My hon. friend talks
about paying the cost of the road. Does he mean that whatever statement the present owners of the road put in as the cost of the road would be accepted, or does he mean that the cost would be based upon what it could have been built for? This road may have been built, for all we know, along the same lines as the Canadian Northern was built. Certain men who owned the road taking the contract and switching it to 25 or 30 per cent of the money they were getting for building the road, thus making private profit.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
Tenders were made and contracts let; the prices must have been reasonable, because some of the contractors failed with the work and other contractors had to take it up and complete it. The amount that is to be paid is the amount that actually went into the road, the right of way, and terminals. The judge of the Exchequer Court is the man to decide whether the statements submitted to him are correct as to the money expended on this railway. No person will put in accounts by which there will be any money made out of this transaction. The information I have is that these lines will serve quite a population in that locality. I am informed that in the county of Charlevoix there are 22,000 people without railway accommodation. This line enters the county of Chicoutimi and Saguenay and will be of service to a number of people in that district. The population of that county is some 65,000, as shown by the census. It will serve the county of Montmorency, which has a population of 15,000, and it will be of benefit to the city of Quebec, the population of which is about 90,000. It will also be of benefit to the people in Quebec county, of which the population is 27,000. My view is that this road will be of considerable benefit to the neople along The north shore, who should have had railway accommodation before this. Part of this road has been in operation for many years and has been of great benefit to those who have had the advantage of that operation, as is shown by the earnings that I have given. The line from the end of Quebec and Montmorency to

Murray Bay, will, I believe, have good earning power. Very many people go down to Murray Bay and along the north shore during the summer. A great many people, many of them farmers, live along that route, and to them this line will be of great benefit. I discussed this matter with our railway management, and they believe that the road will be quite an advantage to our transcontinental system. Having regard to all the conditions, I have no hesitation in recommending that this road be purchased and put in operation at the earliest possible date.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
What about
the railway on the south shore?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: There is a short line, about 30 miles in length.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Is that a branch of the Intercolonial?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
Yes, it is a branch line of
the Intercolonial, it is on the south side.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
It is not a branch line
yet.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: It will be when we acquire it.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
What I mean is, does
it connect with the Intercolonial?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Yes. As I have shown, the earnings are not very large, but they are on the right side, and this line will be a feeder to the Intercolonial.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Why does not the minister allow that to come under the statute^of 1915, which provides for taking over branch lines of the Intercolonial?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
Even if we did take it over
under the Branch Lines Act, we would have to come to Parliament and have the transaction confirmed; therefore we might just as well bring it in now and include it in this legislation. We are really bringing it in under the legislation to which my hon. friend refers, and confirming it at the same time. As this line connects with the Intercolonial, we could have brought it in under the branch line legislation, as the hon. member suggests, but we would have to come to Parliament for the other two lines in any case. The Prime Minister assured the House that if any roads were taken over under that Act which were not in connection with the Intercolonial, he would come to Parliament and have the acquiring of them confirmed as we are doing.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
The road on the south
side of the St. Lawrence does not come within the minister's- promise to my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, because that would come under the statute of 1915. By this Bill the minister is making an entirely different provision. Under the Act of 1915, an agreement had been come to as to the price; but here he is providing that, these two roade shall be picked out, an exception made in their case, and the price to be paid is to be fixed by the Exchequer Court. Whether or not the Government may deem that price to be reasonable, they will be bound to pay. That is (the difference, and I think it is very exceptional and favourable treatment that is being afforded to these two Toads as compared with the roads enumerated in the statute of 1915.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Of course we could do as the hon. gentleman says; but this is just as convenient and I cannot see that it is not in the interest of the Government to do it in this way.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Does the minister not see that he is simply appointing another commission? It is this pernicious practice of appointing commissions; he is making the Exchequer Court a commission. Is it not possible for the minister to bargain for anything?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: It is not fair for the hon. gentleman to make that statement. The Exchequer Court was organized for the purpose of settling any claim that any person might have against the Government, or to adjust matters if the Government is purchasing.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: The minister need not explain to me what the Exchequer Court is; I know that quite well.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: If the hon. member knows, it is not fair to make the statement he has made. I believe that every hon. member in this House will be satisfied that, whatever decision the Exchequer Court makes in connection with these roads or any other matters that may come before the court.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: But you tie up the Exchequer Court with conditions.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
Only in . so far as the maximum amount to be paid is concerned; and I think it is right, in the interests of the Government to do so, because we say that the actual cost is not to exceed a certain amount. The statement is made to the
Government that there has been a very much larger amount than this expended on the road, and for that reason we say: We will limit the amount to this maximum. If, when the statements are put before the judge of the Exchequer Court, he is of the opinion that there has not been this amount expended on these Toads, then he has power to fix a lower price: That is the reason we limit the maximum.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Has my hon. friend taken any steps to verify the figures given to him of how much has been put into the road? He says it has been stated that more than this amount has been put into it. I presume that statement has been made by the company, that they have expended more than appears. Has any audit been made, and have these figures been verified?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: No, we have not gone that far because we have the figures showing what has been paid. We feel perfectly satisfied that, as the whole matter has to come before the Exchequer Court, ',he court will take good care to see that that amount has actually been expended or has gone into the road; and for that reason it would hardly be necessary for us to go that far. We have confidence in the Exchequer Court carrying out the provisions of the Act.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: The Exchequer Court, tc put it shortly, was established to decide claims of contractors. A contractor does not go to the Exchequer Court and say: I spent so much. The Exchequer Court decides certain disputes under his contract. If the Government were expropriating a building, the Exchequer Court would decide what the building was worth, not what it cost for its construction, although that might be an element in the evidence. What I mean by tying up the Court is that the Government is compelling it to take what was put into the road as a basis, even if one-half of what was put into it has floated away. Suppose the road had been constructed, and a million dollars worth of it had been washed away.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: They have got to reproduce it.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
That is all right. My hon. friend ties up the Exchequer Court to give a decision based on the amount that was invested. Unless in their judgment value was received for that investment, the basis is no good at all. Suppose the road were extravagantly built, supposing, for reasons that occur sometimes in railway construction, it cost the company one

million dollars and they got value for only one-half a million dollars, there is no provision made for an allowance for that in the Exchequer Court. The judge must take into account what they expended. The basis ought to be the value of the work that is there, no matter what it cost. That, I think, would be the simple way. The Exchequer Court should not be tied up as is here proposed.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Does the hon. member mean the value based upon the cost at the time of construction, or what, if it were constructed to-day, that same work would be worth?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: The judge ought to have full liberty to take everything into consideration.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Then you are opening it up to a dangerous point.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: If the Government is going to pay the value and no more or less, the judge ought to be the one to determine what the value is. If you take the road as a going concern-my hon. friend need not be alarmed-portions of it have a high value. I am pointing out that the minister is tying up the Exchequer Court on a certain basis on which the court will bring in its findings, and that is not a correct basis; it ought to be the value of the property at present, no matter what it cost.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: My idea is that the present value might be a great deal more than its cost when constructed; and if it is opened up in that way, the country may pay a great deal more than the money put in to build the road.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that will not be the case.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: I wish to remind hon. members that the question before the House is the second reading of the Bill.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
I think I appreciate the point raised by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham). His contention is that no special limit should be placed upon the Exchequer Court in determining the value; that the Exchequer Court should be governed by the same conditions as it is governed by in other matters when values come before it for determination. It is well known that, under the law governing expropriations, the Exchequer Court considers the various elements, all in varying degree, depending on the case that happens to be before it; sums those elements up and

reaches a valuation. What these elements are and what the law is, there is no need to dilate upon; it is well known to hon. gentlemen opposite. If in this case no basis were provided for the Exchequer Court, it would be difficult, if not indeed impossible, to arrive at a determination. As the hon. minister has stated, the intimation that a basis of value would be desirable came from the Exchequer Court itself. I can quite understand why such an intimation should come in this case. Ordinarily the basis of allowance by an Exchequer Court, or indeed by any court, on an expropriation; is the damage .done to the parties from whom the property is expropriated, and the damage would be the value of the property to that party; the loss he suffers by its severance from him and by its being taken to become the property of the expropriator. It naturally would appear to the judge of the Exchequer Court that in this case it would be very difficult to have any means of arriving at a basis where all these elements would come in. Here is a road for example, the Quebec and Saguenay, 62:8 miles, which runs through a country yet unprovided with railways, which has been built at a very great expense on account of the character of the country through which it runs. That railway if it were completed, would serve a certain population that exists there to-day. I do not know how the value of that railway could be estimated. It is a matter of potentiality. It is a matter of estimating the future, of estimating, not only the conditions that prevail now, while the railway is in embryo, but of estimating what may be the prospects of the road as conditions develop by the operation of the railway itself. It may be that the railway handled by the company in whose hands it is, would be a losing proposition for a time. One man might say that it would be a losing proposition always; another might say differently. There would be nothing of a tangible nature to go upon, because it is a matter, not of existing conditions, but of potentialities that are buried in the nature of the conditions themselves.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
I understand that we
are not expropriating this railway, but taking over the road for what it may be worth?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: It is not in the nature of an expropriation but of a purchase?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
That is true in one
sense. While I am on the point, I may answer the hon. gentleman in full. The Act of 1915, under which we are empowered to act, gives the minister the power to take over a road, and under a clause in that Act, he may exercise all the powers of expropriation. That power is given in a clause on the second page of the Act, if my hon. friend will turn it up. The minister is not required to exercise the powers of expropriation, but he has the powers of expropriation vested in him by that statute.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
You are not going
to exercise them here?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
Oh, yes; we will have the power to exercise them as soon as this Bill passes, because we take the roads under the provisions " of an Act to amend the Government Railways Act and to authorize the purchase of certain railways." Taking the road under that, we get the powers of that Act, and we would be able to exercise the power of expropriation. But whether we choose to exercise it or not, or whether we choose to make an agreement by way of purchase with the necessary provisions for the protection of the Government, and then refer that agreement, either under the Act of this session, or simply under this Act, the [DOT]course before the Exchequer Court would be to determine the value of the road, the valye of what we get, and under the very peculiar circumstances that prevail here, expropriating a railway, part of which is only a railway in embryo, the ordinary rules would he very difficult, indeed, of application. Consequently, it appeared to the judge of that court that a basis of valuation was essential.
Before I deal with the method of arriving at a basis, I may say that the words I have used so far apply pretty accurately, also, to the first thirty miles of the Montmorency and Charlevoix road. That road also has a certain value now. But it may have a much greater value when the addition is completed, the Quebec and Saguenay railway, which connects it up with Naim Falls. It may have an added value by virtue of the possibility of the extension of that line to St. Catherines Bay, which is claimed to be a winter port.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: I said what is claimed to be a winter port; I am not giving a decision, because I have not the evidence of my own judgment on that matter which the hon. member for Assiniboia apparently has.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: I lived until I was grown up 100 miles east of that point on the St. Lawrence river, where you could not see across the river, and there was no winter port there, but solid ice all the winter through.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: It may be a long time since my hon. friend was there.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: It is a long time, about forty years.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Conditions might have changed.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Would it not be well to ascertain whether conditions have changed?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: It would be before we build the road. We are not holding out the prospect of building it yet. What the hon. member has said only illustrates and emphasizes the point I am making, the very great difference of opinion as to prospects. There would be nothing substantial and tangible upon which the Exchequer Court could proceed in estimating the value of a potentiality like that.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
You could trust the
judge.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: We do trust the judge? That is what we are asking the House to do, and the judge asks that Parliament fix a basis, and we propose to trust his judgment in making that request.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: How is the amount arrived at?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
I will explain that. In arriving at a basis, in getting at something that would be a basis, we had in mind these considerations: The road has been built by a private company. It was intended to be built for gain. The presumption is that they would build it to the best advantage; consequently, it would be clear [DOT]that even under ordinary conditions the actual cost of the road, not necessarily the [DOT]bonded indebtedness, but the actual money that was translated into the road would be a very important consideration to the judge. However, the fact also appeared that this part of the road had been constructed for some time, and there would be depreciation, and we knew by virtue of our own officers' reports that there would be wash-

outs and the like. Consequently, it was essential that depreciation should be taken off. I think it also right that the subsidies should be taken off, and the actual money that went in, and is now buried in the road, less that depreciation and less the subsidies, would be the value.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: The depreciation for wear and tear during the time the road was lying idle.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: There is tear perhaps, but not wear, because the road has not been used. As to the way the amount is fixed, that is the amount they offer the road at, but not having proof, and not wishing to assume the responsibility of saying that that amount of money has gone into the road, and that there is not sufficient depreciation to make it less than that now, we refer that to the Exchequer Court; but we put a limitation because we do not wish the amount to exceed that at which the company are ready now to dispose of it. I think that that answers all the questions which have been raised.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: I have been looking over the amendment which the Acting Minister of Railways said he would propose, and I would like to know whether it applies to the whole three railroads or to the first two only.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: To the three.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Let me read the amendment.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: I have seen it.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
It strikes me as very peculiar. (Reads):
The said value to be the actual cost of said railways less depreciation, but- not to exceed $4,465,000, exclusive of outstanding bonded indebtedness which is to be assumed by the Government, but not to exceed in all $2,500,000.
That is, the value of the three railroads should be fixed by the Exchequer Court, but it is not to exceed $6,965,000. That applies to the three railroads?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Are they all owned by the same company?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: They seem to be separate corporations.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
I would not like to get involved in a discussion as to title, because it is very involved, I can assure the hon. gentleman; but the stock, I understand, is

pretty much controlled by the same company, and the intention is that the value of the whole three railroads shall be arrived at by that process. The $2,500,000 are long distance bonds at a low rate of interest, which, I understand, there is no object at all in paying off. They will stand against the Montmorency and Charlevoix Railway. The whole valuation will be taken, and the . equity in the whole, over and above that $2,500,000, must not exceed $4,465,000.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
I have no objection to urge against the Government acquiring these railways, because I have not sufficient knowledge of the country, or of the railways themselves, to enable me to express an opinion. Therefore, I do not wish to be understood as opposing the acquisition of these railways. That is a matter in regard to which, as far as I am concerned, the Government must be answerable to the House. But one thing that seems to me to require explanation is why this mode of taking over the roads has been adopted. It differs very materialy from the provision made by Parliament in the year 1915 for the taking over of branch lines for the Intercolonial. In that Act it is provided that no branch line shall be taken over unless in the opinion of the minister it can "more conveniently and usefully be operated as a part of the Government Railway system, or which might be deemed necessary or desirable for the more efficient operation of the said system." The Government could not take over any branch line pf the Intercolonial unless in the minister's opinion it fulfilled either one or the other of these conditions. But in this case Parliament is asked expressly to authorize the minister to acquire these three roads with the approval of the Governor General in Council.
There is another very great distinction. In the Act of 1915 the purchase is to be a matter of bargain between the Government and the railway company. In this case the Government seems to abdicate altogether its function of determining the price which it will pay to these companies, it being provided that the Government shall pay whatever the Judge of the Exchequer Court might deem a proper amount. And this amendment absolutely ties the hands of the Judge of the Exchequer Court by providing that he shall be bound to allow the actual cost of the railways less depreciation.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Not the actual cost.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Yes, it says so.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: A maximum amount is fixed.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
But not exceeding so
much. It does not give the judge of the Exchequer Court or the Government any discretion to take the roads over at a price which it would be reasonable for the Government to pay. In that respect it is different from the Act of 1915, which leaves the discretion entirely to the judgment of the Governor in Council. We know very well that there may be many railroads-we have some in New Brunswick-whose owners would be delighted to get one-hali the actual amounts which those roads cost. It is perfectly well understood that the Government had no intention of paying what the roads cost, but would insist on getting them at a valuation which would be likely in the not distant future to yield at all events some return, even though it might be small, on the money invested by the Government. For some reason the Government is making a departure from the Act of 1915 and is specifying that so long as the actual cost Qf these roads, outside of the bonded indebtedness, does not exceed $4,466,000 the judge of the Exchequer Court shall be bound to allow that amount, even though the roads may cost twice as much as might have been reasonably and necessarily expended on the construction, and even the condition of the roads may be such as to require the expenditure of a very large amount of money to put them in a reasonably fit condition for traffic. I think some explanation should be given why the Government is departing from the provisions of the Act of 1915. It does seem to me that if the Government is going to leave this matter to the Exchequer Court it should at all events provide that the amount should not exceed the actual reasonable and necessary cost of the construction of the lines. Those are the words which Parliament has adopted in reference to subsidies. As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, Parliament provides that where the cost of a railroad exceeds $15,000 per mile the Government may grant an additional subsidy upon the cost of the road up to $21,000, so as to allow of a subsidy of $6,400 a mile being granted. Parliament does not allow that increased -subsidy to be given on the actual cost, but stipulates that it shall only be given on the actual, reasonable and necessary cost of the construction of the line. It does seem to me that if the gentlemen who own these roads are desirous of getting rid of them, or of transferring to the Government the burden 252i
of completing and operating them, they ought to be satisfied to take what the Judge of the Exchequer Court would deem to be the actual, reasonable and necessary cost of construction. That I think would be a reasonable proposition to make. My contention, therefore, is that the Government, instead of coming down here with a separate Bill providing in respect of these roads provisions entirely different from those which obtain in the Branch Lines Act of 1915, should have amended that Act of 1915 to make it apply to branch lines of the Transcontinental as well. That would have been a simple proposition. While I am on my feet I desire, with all due respect, and in all kindness, to say to the Minister of Railways that there will be a very strong feeling of disappointment among the people of the province from which I come that, before- carrying out the provisions of the Act of 1915, which provides -for the taking over of branch lines of the Intercolonial, the Government is bringing down now a provision for the taking over of two new lines which were not contemplated by Parliament at that time, and with respect to the taking over of which no provision was made. I wish my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was in his place. He ought to be as deeply interested in this matter as I am, for his constituents are very deeply interested in this question. As long ago as the year 1911, before the general elec-tins, the hon. member for Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler) sent a hurried S.O.S. call from St. John or Sussex to the then leader of the Opposition, now the Prime Minister, and who was then in Charlottetown, asking in most pressing terms for the views of the	right hon. gentleman
with regard to the taking over of branch lines	of the Intercolonial.
It is stated that it was the policy of the Conservative party to take over all those branch lines of the Intercolonial which could be operated to advantage in connection with the Intercolonial. In New Brunswick, there are quite a number of branch lines, the taking over of which has been agitated for a good many years, and the people in the various counties interested were delighted to receive from the then leader of the Opposition that assurance which was published broadcast in the Conservative newspapers and which, no doubt, had a very reassuring effect upon the people. Hon. gentlemen can realize how much it would influence the people of the constituencies interested in

voting in favour of the hon. member for Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler) and other Conservative candidates. There is a railroad running from Hampton to St. Martins, only some thirty miles in length. There is a railway in York county known as the York and Cqrleton railway. There is a railway in Kings county known as the Elgin, Petit Codiac and Havelock railway. There is another railway called the Harvey and Salisbury railway. >
There is another railway known, as the Moncton and Buc-touche railway, and another from Kent Junction to Richibucto known as the Northern railway.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Those are all old timers.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
There is. one from Bathurst to Tracadie in the county of Gloucester; and there are also some in Nova Scotia and some in Quebec. The people interested have been looking for years for the taking over of those branch lines. What I complain of is that these pre-election promises should be regarded just as the Kaiser regarded the treaty which it was thought would preserve the neutrality of Belgium, that is, that they should be regarded as mere scraps of paper which the Conservative party could break at will. I am sorry the hon. member for Kings and Albert and also the Minister of Marine and Fisheries are not here, because their constituencies are interested in this question. They felt that before entering upon new engagements, these old, timeworn promises of the Conservative party ought to be carried'out. The taking over of all these branch lines that I have mentioned would hot cost anything like the amount which it is proposed to expend on these three railroads which are mentioned in the Bill before the House to-night.
Before I take my seat I want to call attention to the extraordinary statement which my hon. friend the Solicitor General has made to-night, that this amendment is made at the suggestion of the judge of the Exchequer Court. Let me ask how it is that the judge of the Exchequer Court would make a suggestion of that kind before such a Bill is passed, before any proceedings are taken or could by any possibility have been taken in the Exchequer Court. How is it that he could make a suggestion as to the amendment to be made in this Bill and that the Government is not acting upon its own judgment, but upon a suggestion made by that judge? Perhaps the Solicitor General will enlighten us on that?
[Mr. Pugsley.l

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Perhaps we had better get into committee, as I have already spoken.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: I would not like my hon. friend to get out of order, because that would be bad. Not many days ago the Minister of Justice told the House that in his opinion it would be quite impossible for Parliament to constitute this Royal Commission presided over by Chief Justice Meredith and Mr. Justice Duff into a court which would enable them to make inquiries and to issue commissions for the purpose of making inquiries. Almost at the very time that the minister was making that statement, there either stood upon the Order Paper, or had been been passed, a Bill which provided that this Exchequer Court, without having any expropriation proceedings before it, might make inquiries as to the value of property which the Government might think of buying or selling. None of us thought at that time of the purpose for which that Bill was introduced. It appears now that it was introduced and that it has been passed1 for the very purpose of enabling values to be placed upon those railways which the House is being called upon to consider to-night. I have no doubt whatever that the action of the Minister of Justice, in proposing that Bill to the House and having it passed, has been in anticipation of the railroad legislation which we are now being called upon to consider. Ft may be, of course, that the attention of the judge of the Exchequer Court was called to that Bill when it passed, and possibly that may be the explanation why he has given this information to my hon, friend.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: That was not it at all.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
I can certainly conceive of no other explanation of the judge of the Exchequer Court obtruding his views upon the Government before any question relating to the subject had come before him. There are no expropriation proceedings before him; there is no intimation; there is no proceeding of any kind. or description, and there could be no proceedings of any kind or description before the judge of the Exchequer Court which would justify or explain his making any intimation to the Government, and I can only imagine it is done because the previous Act which has been passed by this Parliament at the instance of the hon. Minister of Justice has been brought to his attention and he has been informed that it was intended to act

with regard to these railways. That would be an explanation why this amendment has been suggested. I can think of no other.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
As two of these railways run through a country with which I am tolerably familiar, I think it is incumbent upon me to give a few words of explanation to the House. As to the railway which runs from St. Jean des Chaillons on the St. Lawrence to Lyster on the Grand Trunk and further north to the intersection of the Intercolonial, I am not so familiar. It runs through the county of Lotbiniere and also through a part of the county of Me-gantic. For the most part it runs through very good timber land, and I have no doubt that if it is properly managed and operated, it will prove a good feeder for the Intercolonial.
I am more familiar with the topography of the country through which the other two railways run. The old Quebec and Montmorency railway runs from Quebec to St. Joachim, through part of the county of Quebec and through part of the county of Montmorency, my old constituency. This runs through parishes which are prosperous and uniformly populous, through what is known as La C6te Beaupre. There is practically one continuous village from the station at Quebec down to St. Joachim.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: Is that the electric railway that runs down to Montmorency Falls?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
Yes; that railway
passes first through the parish of Beau-port which is a very prosperous parish in the county of Quebec.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
Who operates the road at
present?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
The Quebec Railway,
Light, Heat and Power Company, which holds the Quebec street railway also, and which, I believe, is the holding company for this other company, the Lotbiniere and Me-gantic. It then passes through a parish named St. Gregoire below Montmorency falls. It also has a line on the ridge which runs to the upper part of Beauport three or four miles from Quebec, to the Kent House at the Falls. The lower line, after leaving the parish of St. Gregoire, runs through the populous parish of L'Ange Gardien, and through the large parish of Chateau Richer, thence to and through the town of Ste. Anne de Beaupre, where, as hon. members are aware, there is a famous shrine, to which thousands of pilgrims go every year, especially in the summer. It then runs
through the parish of St. Joachim which is the terminus of the old Quebec and Montmorency railway. From this the line proceeds to Petite Riviere St. Frangois, through a country that is sparsely populated and most difficult for railway construction, on account of its mountainous character, but eomingdown to this parish of Petite Riviere St. Frangois, there are two populous parishes on the brow of the hill-St. Tite, which is a mile and a half from the river, and St. Fereol three miles from St. Tite. These must have a population combined of 3,000. There is a considerably wooded country there, and no doubt if the railway is run through the region it will have quite a freight as well as a passenger business. Then, from the parish of Petite Riviere St. Frangois we go on to the populous parish of Baie St. Paul with from 2,500 to 3,000 population, including the parish of St. Urbain. Then, passing along the shore of the St. Lawrence, we come to Les Eboulements and St. Irenee, famous watering places, and then to Murray Bay. This place has been known for many years as a famous watering place and its reputation is increasing every year. I have no doubt that if a railway were run to that point, there would be traffic along the line in lumber and timber; while at Baie St. Paul and also at Murray Bay there would be industries of various kinds.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: What kind of timber is it?

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
Pulpwood, there are large quantities of it. This country has never been provided with railway communication. A combined railway and steamer route was established some
11 p.m. years ago by which Murray Bay could be reached. At great expense the Government built a spur line from the Intercolonial railway from St. Pacome to Riviere Ouelle, where communication is maintained with Murray Bay for six months in the year; but for the other six months communication is greatly interrupted by the ice, the winds, and the snow storms on the St. Lawrence. Sp this population is almost completely deprived of any communication except by stage coach with the city of Quebec. It seems to me that we can profit by the experience gained by the building of the Lake St. John railway. The climate, soil and general characteristics of the country through which this line of railway will run may be compared with that served by the Lake St. John railway. Before the railway was built to Lake St. John there was only 10,000 of a population in that region. There is to-day a population of

almost 100,000, and when I was up there last summer I was surprised at the statistics handed to me showing the exports from that region-cereals, dead meat, cattle, and all kinds of farm products. It is now a rich country, and hon. members will be surprised to find in that northern part of the province so rich a region. There is no reason why the same development should not take place in the region to be served by the railway which it is proposed to purchase if this Bill goes through. A great deal of money has been spent in the construction of the railway from St. Joachim to Murray Bay, and the line has been to a great extent ballasted, and was at one time ready for the rails. Vast sums of money have been expended on this enterprise. When one takes into consideration the fact that this part of the country has always been deprived of railroad communication, why should we not conclude that it is time that the population of the north shore of the St. Lawrence should have the same measure of assistance that other parts of the country have received? There has been a question as to the amendment proposed by the Minister of Railways. It seems to me that the proper time for discussing the meaning of that amendment is when the Bill is in Committee of the Whole. I have no objection, of course, to the very enlightening observations made by hon. gentlemen opposite, *especially those of my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley). But, if I am not mistaken, the suggestion of the amendment came because a case of this kind had been before the Exchequer Court, and it was found necessary to put wording of this kind into the Bill to meet difficulties such as were encountered in that case. I have forgotten at the moment the name of that case. The amount to be paid is to be an amount ascertained after full investigation by the Exchequer Court. This is the security which the Government gives to the country that no fanciful amount will be paid for the railway, but only its real value to the country. The Bill should go to the committee and then we can discuss more completely and with fuller information the wording of the amendment proposed.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
I desire to point out one feature of this proposal which strikes me, and that is that the Government seem to have no confidence in their own administration. This evening the Minister of Railways asked for and obtained a vote of

$150,000 to provide the expense of a commission to inquire into the railway situation, and the Minister of Finance made a very pressing speech, and gave to the House the impression that the Government were considering the nationalization of all railways in Canada. Scarcely had this $150,000 been voted to- inquire into the railway situation in Canada when the Acting Minister of Railways asked for the passage of a Bill to acquire three railways. Is it because he lacked confidence in the commission that is to be appointed? It seems to me that the logical, business way of going about this would be to await the report of the proposed commission so that we should have full information concerning these railways which we propose taking over, as to their earning value, the country through which they are going, and so on, and be in a position to decide whether or not it would be profitable for Canada to take them over and hitch them up with the Government railway system. I submit that for the consideration of the acting minister.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext: I wish to correct some statistics I gave a moment ago concerning Baie St. Paul. I said that the population aggregated about 3,000. I am told that the aggregate population of the town and parish of Baie St. Paul is now over 5,000.

subtopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS ACQUISITION OF BRANCH LINES.
speechtext:
We have been discussing the railroad situation in Canada for a couple of days. We have had before us the question of the two transcontinental railways. We have had information to the effect that the resources of Canada are being strained to the limit in the effort to carry these enterprises to completion and over the present difficult financial situation of the country. Every suggestion that has been made as to the lack of satisfactory character in the proposals of the Government with regard to those railroads has been met by the assertion that the country could not afford more money; that the financial resources of the country were being strained to the limit to meet the needs of these great enterprises in which the whole credit of the country and its future welfare was involved. As my hon. friend the member for Huntingdon said a few moments ago, just as soon as these two proposals were adopted, the Acting Minister of Railways comes forward with a proposition which would argue that Canada had money to throw to the birds; *that there wa6 no lack of money in Canada for railroad propositions. A proposal is

being submitted to Parliament to-day such [DOT]as never was submitted before in the history of this country. Nothing was ever submitted that would approach this proposition in its character, and certainly the country never was in such a condition as it is to-day, eo ill prepared to deal with a proposal of this kind. We have no money to adjust matters with the Grand Trunk or with the Canadian Northern that would enable the traffic of this country to be carried, but we have $4,500,000 that we can pay out in cash, 'we will assume $2,500,000 of bonds and we will be prepared to spend anything from $1,000,000 to $5,000,000 in cash in respect of a railroad of the length of 135 miles. That of itself is a very fair order, but when we remember that of the 135 miles of railroad that is proposed to be dealt with, .30 miles has been completed for I do not know how long, is in operation, is serving the purpose for which it was built, has no connection with the other railroad with which it is associated, has no legitimate claim upon this country, we must come to the conclusion that there is no reason in the world why this railroad should be taken over by the country except that at the present time presumably it does not earn interest on its bonds and the owners deem it desirable that the country should assume the responsibility of paying that shortage of interest. The same condition applies to a portion at any rate, if not the whole of the Quebec and Montmorency railroad, a railroad which has been in operation for years, doing a large business, paying its operating expenses with some surplus, but not enough to pay interest on its bonds. This railroad has no claim whatever on the country in any shape, form or manner except the claim that the owners of the property desire this country to pay for them that which they are not able to earn and pay for themselves. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that no such proposal	was	ever brought before	the
Parliament of Canada as in the cases	that I have mentioned, the
Lotbiniere railway and the Quebec and Montmorency railway. The lines are completed, the country has no responsibility, whatever in respect of them; they are in operation. We are asked, at a time when money is more needed than ever it was before, for more urgent purposes than it ever was required before, to hand out mil. lions for the purpose simply of relieving the proprietors of these two properties of
the losses of interest which they are carrying at the present time.
There is also a demand that we shall assume responsibility for completion of .62 miles of uncompleted road of the Quebec and Saguenay line. This road is partially completed; .grading is done, I understand, to the extent of 85 per cent. We are to pay for this work that has been done, and by so doing we are assuming the responsibility for completing the enterprise whatever the cost may be. While the Acting Minister of Railways suggested that the Toad was 85 per cent completed and that ?1,000,000 would be necessary to complete the 60 odd miles, it has been suggested to me that $2,000,000 or $3,000,000 would be very much nearer the requirement to secure completion of the line. The Postmaster General has put before the House the claims of the people who are living along the line of these two railroads. He has stated their numbers. He has given, I presume, the most favourable facts with regard to their requirements. We do not need to discuss the railroad situation there. No doubt the people of that locality desire railroad communication. No doubt they need railroad communication; no doubt railroad communication would be vastly to their advantage. But there are throughout this broad' Dominion thousands of instances where an equal number of people are needing railroad communication just as much as these people are, and where that railroad communication would not cost a fraction of what it will cost in this case.
Then, let it be remembered that these people who will benefit by the construction of this railroad have, during the whole summer season, the advantage of deep water navigation along the whole line. That is to say, they are not at all in the same position as the people living on the St. John railway line. That country was altogether isolated from communication until the St. John railway was built. These people are living along the shores of the St. Lawrence and they have boat communication all season long. So, while they are under a disadvantage during the winter, they are not at all in the same position as people dwelling in an inland locality who have not the advantage of river navigation. The amount of traffic that is to be carried by this railroad, supposing it is completed, has not been represented by the Postmaster General. It may be large; but I submit that the fact that neither of the two completed railroad sections included in the pro-

position earns interest on its cost of construction, is fair evidence that this extension of one of them would be in exactly the same position, if not in a very much woTse position because of the higher cost of construction and the smaller volume of traffic available to support that cost. It seems to me that the Minister of Finance, who is the guardian of the treasury-and no one will say that he is not, under ordinary circumstances, an efficient guardian- should be heard from upon this proposition. He has told us how he has limited the aid to be given by the Government to the two great transcontinental railway enterprises, whose success is of vital importance to every man, woman and child in the Dominion, and while he spoke of having been successful in restricting the amounts they are to receive from the Dominion treasury to the limit before the House, he is a party to the placing before Parliament of a< proposal that will, on the face of it, call for more money than the proposal that he brought before this House as regards the Transcontinental railway, and more than half as much as the proposal which he places before this House in regard to the Canadian Northern railway. Where is my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) P Surely he should be heard from on this occasion. Surely if it is unfair to the country and to the- Treasury to make these proposed loans to the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern railroad, to serve great national enterprises for great national purposes, it must foe a far greater wrong to spend this vast amount of money for the purpose of relieving certain gentlemen, no doubt very creditable gentlemen, no doubt very enterprising gentlemen against whom nothing in the world is to be said. Why should they be relieved of their unfortunate responsibility any more than anybody else? Why should these gentlemen have the preference over every other man and every other enterprise throughout the country that has happened to make miscalculations, or possibly to have fallen on evil days. I think the Minister of Finance and the member for Calgary, and our other friends on the opposite side of the House who have been so insistent on protecting the treasury and the rights and interests of the people of Canada during the past few days, should be heard from very strongly in regard to this proposal, which 
certainly, I think I am safe in saying, is unique in the history of Canada.

Very good;
then, do not bring it up. I have here the report of some engineers; but I do not see a word of the correspondence that has passed between the company and the Government. We ought to have that correspondence so that we can see the reasons why the Government have been induced to take up that road. I do not imagine that the Government have come to a decision on a matter of this kind without having some facts placed before them by the company. Then we are told by the minister that he had the matter submitted to his engineers or the officials of this department and that they recommended the purchase of the road; that the officers in their report highly approved of it. There is not a word of these reports in the papers that have been brought down. Then the minister has told us that the road is not yet completed, that there are some 16 miles still to finish. There are no specifications of the work to be done; not a word of specification, and before we commit ourselves to the building of the road we ought to have a specification as to its character, as to stations, tracking, and so on. Then there are rivers along that line- I do not know how many, but there are a few-and there is no statement as to whether bridges have been constructed or not. Before we take up the matter again, I think we have the right to expect that all this information will be brought down.
